GAP-01.speaker: marigold
GAP-01.text: No list of the 72 papers judged relevant at the 2023 full-text stage (E.2.9, gap 1). The screening log gives the count only; the nearest artefact, the EndNote export of 27 January 2023, holds 79 records, not 72.

GAP-01-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-01-ans.text: That's right, and I set it out myself in E.2.9. Every file in the archive was searched. The 2023 manuscript, the one I submitted to MDPI Future Transportation in March 2023, gives the same counts but no list of the 72 either. What survives is the EndNote export of 79 records, the 49 plus 30 others, and in 2026 I assessed every one of those 30, plus Kanter, against the 2023 criteria, so every paper that could have been among the 23 dropped now has a recorded decision and reason (E.2.10).

GAP-02.speaker: marigold
GAP-02.text: No reasons recorded for the 23 papers dropped between the 72 and the 49 (E.2.9, gap 2). The record gives only four topic labels.

GAP-02-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-02-ans.text: The 2023 record gives reasons by topic, not paper by paper: crowd-shipping, travelling salesman problems, bicycle deliveries and public transport sharing. My MDPI manuscript of March 2023 gives those same four labels and no per-paper reasons, so the gap stands. That's why I re-ran the stage in 2026: each candidate coded twice against the 2023 criteria, every disagreement settled, agreement on subject 30 of 31, alpha .91. Twenty-nine exclusions stand, and the two papers that meet the criteria, Casado-Vara (2020), a model, and Marcucci (2021), an encyclopedia chapter, aren't of a kind the 49 lack.

GAP-03.speaker: marigold
GAP-03.text: No per-paper reasons at Stage 3 (title and abstract, 333 removed) or Stage 5 (full reading, 166 removed): both are totals per database with no titles behind them; Stage 4 names journals, not papers (E.2.9, gap 3).

GAP-03-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-03-ans.text: Those can't be reconstructed from the 2023 files, and I don't pretend they can. What I could do was make the update transparent where the original wasn't: in 2026 I ran the original string again in OpenAlex alongside five corrected strings and logged a decision and a reason for every one of the 1,535 records, and I re-ran the full-text stage of 2023 paper by paper.

GAP-04.speaker: marigold
GAP-04.text: The surviving full-text database holds 237 rows where the screening log says 238 (E.2.9, gap 4).

GAP-04-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-04-ans.text: One record is missing and the file doesn't show which. I used the 237-row table as it stands, to de-duplicate the 2026 screen against it, and not to reconstruct any decision: its screening columns are almost entirely empty, so it can't carry a decision trail anyway.

GAP-05.speaker: marigold
GAP-05.text: The 2023 manuscript says four screening stages; the spreadsheet runs five and numbers them differently (E.2.9, gap 5).

GAP-05-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-05-ans.text: Not a gap in the data, but they won't line up if quoted side by side, so I say so. The manuscript's four stages are its exclusion steps, starting with duplicates; the spreadsheet also numbers the keyword search and download as Stage 1, so it runs to five. The spreadsheet is the one with the counts, so the thesis follows its five stages.

GAP-06.speaker: marigold
GAP-06.text: The 860 records count the eight hand-added pre-2018 papers twice (662 + 198).

GAP-06-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-06-ans.text: Yes. The eight sit both under 'Extra' in the 662 and in the 198 published before 2018. I keep 860 because it's the figure the 2023 manuscript reports, and I explain the double count wherever it appears.

GAP-07.speaker: marigold
GAP-07.text: The 2023 criteria table has two date rules that conflict: 'Papers published between 2010 to February 2023' among the inclusions and 'Papers before 2018' among the exclusions.

GAP-07-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-07-ans.text: Both are recorded as written. The operative rule in the screening log is 2018 onwards, with named earlier papers added back by hand, and that's the rule the counts follow. The update replaced judgement with a stated threshold: an earlier paper is kept only if cited thirty times or more.

GAP-08.speaker: marigold
GAP-08.text: The Stage 5 rule in the screening log says 'eliminating those based on mathematical modelling', yet sixteen of the 49 are models or simulations.

GAP-08-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-08-ans.text: The cell says that, but the included set shows it wasn't applied as written, and the review's own criteria table has no modelling exclusion. So in the 2026 re-run I applied the criteria as Table 1 words them and as the 49 show they were applied: no paper was excluded on a ground one of the 49 also fails. That's why Casado-Vara, a model, meets the criteria in the re-run.

GAP-09.speaker: marigold
GAP-09.text: The 2023 screening was done by the author alone.

GAP-09-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-09-ans.text: It was, and Table 3.3 says so. The 2026 re-run of its full-text stage was coded twice, with every disagreement settled, and every decision in the update was logged with its reason.

GAP-10.speaker: marigold
GAP-10.text: The update's stance counts have limits: the stance assignments were given no second reading; eleven late cards were folded in rather than re-adjudicated; 63 cards rest on abstracts and 8 on records only; 38 verdicts on power were assigned by the thesis's own rule.

GAP-10-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-10-ans.text: All true, and all stated. The cards were read again from the full texts in September 2026, which moved the silence counts but not the direction, but the stance assignments themselves had no second reading. Silence counts are upper bounds, because absence from an abstract isn't absence from the paper. And the power count only shows whom the field assumes decides; the actual test of power is the interviews and the 117 arrangements in 4.5.

GAP-11.speaker: marigold
GAP-11.text: Appendix E names only 27 of the 29 papers in which a carrier begins the collaboration.

GAP-11-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-11-ans.text: The list was drawn from the cards whose initiator line began with 'carrier' before the full texts were read on 22 September 2026; the synthesis counts 29 after that reading, and the record doesn't name the other two. I say so in E.4 and in 2.2.

GAP-12.speaker: marigold
GAP-12.text: The 49 and the 241 were not selected the same way, so comparisons between them set a stricter set beside a looser one.

GAP-12-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-12-ans.text: Yes. The 49 were included after full-text reading; the 241 after title-and-abstract screening and the citation rule, with 170 then read in full. Wherever the two stand together I say which kind each is.

GAP-13.speaker: marigold
GAP-13.text: Three participants did not sign the consent form (B.3): A5, the second participant in A9, and B8, whose consent came at the close of the call.

GAP-13-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-13-ans.text: Every participant was sent the information sheet and the form. Twenty-seven signed; three gave consent verbally and it's on the recording. B8 had been sent the sheet, which says the interview would be recorded and that recording could be declined. The ESRC holds that verbal consent may be ethically preferable in some contexts and should be audio-recorded where possible, and all three are.

GAP-14.speaker: marigold
GAP-14.text: The information sheet and consent form carry template slips: the construction-industry sentence, 'herself', 'Date xx/xx/2024', consent item 6 pointing to detail the sheet lacks, and an opt-out the form doesn't contain.

GAP-14-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-14-ans.text: They're reproduced exactly as approved and as participants received them, and I list every slip myself in B.3. The construction sentence is template wording that describes neither this research nor any use of its data. Approval was given on 22 February 2024 and data collection began after it.

GAP-15.speaker: marigold
GAP-15.text: The information sheet says the principal investigator would transcribe the interviews; 3.3 says the transcripts were made automatically from the recordings.

GAP-15-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-15-ans.text: The transcripts were made automatically from the recordings and kept as made, with timestamps, as McLellan and colleagues advise. The sheet described the plan at the time of approval. I checked every quotation in Chapters 4 and 5 against its transcript myself, and where the transcript was weak I flag it: in A9 the answers were typed in afterwards, so I read it as low confidence throughout.

GAP-16.speaker: marigold
GAP-16.text: The ethics application planned elements the study did not carry through: a survey built on the qualitative findings and analysed by correlation and regression, case studies, and validation of the framework by expert panels.

GAP-16-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-16-ans.text: The survey change is recorded as change 2 in Table 3.8: it opened on the day of approval, ran beside the interviews, and is read descriptively because a self-selected sample supports no estimate beyond itself. The thesis reports no case study and no expert-panel stage: Ghent is a document analysis, not a case study in Yin's sense, and the framework is offered as propositions for others to test. Those two weren't carried through, and I'd say so plainly.

GAP-17.speaker: marigold
GAP-17.text: The survey: a self-selected sample with no response rate and no country; not piloted; the draft's skip not applied; durations jump from '1-3 years' to 'More than 5 years'; respondents may include interviewees; kappa 1.00 on a codebook drawn from the same answers.

GAP-17-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-17-ans.text: All stated in 3.6 and carried into 3.7. That's why the survey is used for scale only: counts and cross-tabulations, no significance test, nothing inferred to a population, and no link of the chain rests on it. Answers given by non-collaborators to collaborator questions are kept and read as past or expected collaboration.

GAP-18.speaker: marigold
GAP-18.text: Only four of the twenty-six interviews speak for a carrier, and two transcripts (B10, B11) lie outside the domain.

GAP-18-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-18-ans.text: Four carrier voices, three from inside a carrier and one as adviser to a cargo-bike operator; the rest have dealt with carriers from across the table for years. Saturation was reached by kind of party, so carriers are the one kind I call thin. B10 and B11 stay in every denominator of twenty-six and their eight rows stay in the 117, both codings mark them silent on most concepts, and no finding rests on them alone.

GAP-19.speaker: marigold
GAP-19.text: Poor or incomplete transcripts: A9 substantially incomplete with answers typed in afterwards; A5 eight minutes of prepared answers; B8 phone audio and limited English; A11's speaker labels give some participant answers to the interviewer.

GAP-19-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-19-ans.text: Each is flagged in the coding files and in Table 4.1, and read with the confidence it deserves: A9 low confidence throughout, A5's 'successes' recorded as proposals. In A11 the timestamps are right and only the labels are wrong, which Appendix H notes.

GAP-20.speaker: marigold
GAP-20.text: The interviewer raised brand in five interviews and relayed earlier participants' positions in several, so agreement across transcripts is partly the interviewer's doing; the author also coded first and wrote the claim the later codings tested.

GAP-20-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-20-ans.text: Brand was declined in all five interviews where I raised it, and I count it as declined, not absent. The coding files mark every theme I introduced or relayed, and none of it is counted as the participant's view. The later codings were made from the transcripts alone, required evidence against, and each half was read twice; and they threw out two of my own clauses. The exposure that remains is mine, and I name it in 3.7.

GAP-21.speaker: marigold
GAP-21.text: Appendix H's binder was assigned once, by hand, so the 95 of 117 carries no agreement figure; rows are accounts, not schemes; coding A counted one city's scheme three times and another once; six rows have no stated binder; the rural row (H.1, 42) is the participant's inference.

GAP-21-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-21-ans.text: All disclosed. The binder has no agreement figure; the initiator was re-checked in both passes of October 2026, 98 of 117, alpha .80. Rows are counted as accounts and the unique-scheme count for the A half is given, 51 to 52. Cells that couldn't be filled are left 'unclear' rather than inferred, and row 42 is flagged as an inference wherever it's used.

GAP-22.speaker: marigold
GAP-22.text: In Appendix L, rule 1a, thin flows as a condition and the 'something crosses' restriction were all set after the first results were seen; several alphas fall below the tentative bar; the planned re-run without unclear rows is not reported; the outcome counts pilots though the procedure named operating alone.

GAP-22-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-22-ans.text: Each is stated where it's used. Every result is reported with and without rule 1a, and without it the holder condition falls short of 0.9, so I say the interviews support the holder only under that rule. The low alphas (penalty .54, stage .59, flows .55, what crosses .65) are reported, each pass is run separately as a replication, and the results I rely on use the firm codes.

GAP-23.speaker: marigold
GAP-23.text: Two counts of the neutral-third-party binder differ: 36 rows in L.6, 35 in Table H.3.

GAP-23-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-23-ans.text: L.6 groups the 'Bound by' column by keyword; Table H.3 assigns one primary binder per row by hand. Both are given side by side, with every class's difference listed in L.6.

GAP-24.speaker: marigold
GAP-24.text: The locker test: networks not matched on quality, price or terms; only 26 ownership periods; drift by sale rests on two changes of owner; the per-pair gradient is not tested; sources may under-record carriers; the second coder could see the first pass's class totals, though not its codes.

GAP-24-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-24-ans.text: All stated. It shows a difference by owner class at one time, consistent with the link but not a test of its per-pair form. I rest on the permutation test that counts each period once, run no regression, and read both changes of owner both ways.

GAP-25.speaker: marigold
GAP-25.text: The Ghent renderings were not checked by a Dutch speaker, and the documents say what the regime allocates and expected, not what happened on the street.

GAP-25-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-25-ans.text: Each rendering was checked against the Dutch, a second independent translation and a dictionary, and the Dutch stands beside every English line in Appendix J. The permit register and the operators weren't read, so the regime's practice, as opposed to its law, is the next study's question; the city's own promised evaluations aren't reported in the 2023 plan either.

GAP-26.speaker: marigold
GAP-26.text: The savings scenario rests mostly on assumptions: eight of thirteen inputs, with no official UK first-attempt failure rate and no UK data on depot trips.

GAP-26-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-26-ans.text: It's a worked example, not a forecast, and it says so. It shows the order of magnitude and which inputs drive it; it reports a low case, a stress case and every formula, and the proper test is a matched-streets design.

GAP-27.speaker: marigold
GAP-27.text: In the claim register, one claim is 'not verified' (No. 202, the page of the QCA thresholds) and two rest on an exploratory coding made once and not reproduced (Nos. 188 and 190).

GAP-27-ans.speaker: marigold
GAP-27-ans.text: They're marked as such rather than hidden. For No. 202 the chapter of Schneider and Wagemann is identified; only the page on which the thresholds are stated couldn't be checked. No. 190's evidence line reads 'not in the chapters', and No. 188's coding is described as made once and not reproduced in the thesis.

GL-Horizontal_collaboration.speaker: marigold
GL-Horizontal_collaboration.text: Horizontal collaboration. An arrangement between two or more organisations at the same point in the supply chain (carriers with carriers, shippers with shippers, or one public body with another) to gain together what none could gain alone, and to be more competitive for having done so.

GL-Shipper.speaker: marigold
GL-Shipper.text: Shipper. The firm that owns and sends goods, such as a manufacturer or retailer that hires a carrier to deliver them.

GL-The_gap.speaker: marigold
GL-The_gap.text: The gap. The shipper side of horizontal collaboration documented but under-examined as a category, and not set beside the carrier side.

GL-The_chain.speaker: marigold
GL-The_chain.text: The chain. The five linked concepts: overlap, the boundary of sharing, the binder, power and the holder.

GL-Link_1_Overlap.speaker: marigold
GL-Link_1_Overlap.text: Link 1: Overlap. Whether two parties compete for the same customers in the same place.

GL-Link_2_The_boundary_of_sharing.speaker: marigold
GL-Link_2_The_boundary_of_sharing.text: Link 2: The boundary of sharing. The line between what is pooled and what is withheld, drawn where the customer relationship begins.

GL-Link_3_Binding.speaker: marigold
GL-Link_3_Binding.text: Link 3: Binding. The arrangement supplied from outside the parties that holds a collaboration where trust between them cannot.

GL-Binder.speaker: marigold
GL-Binder.text: Binder. Whatever holds an arrangement together once it is formed and does not depend on the goodwill of the parties.

GL-Link_4_Power.speaker: marigold
GL-Link_4_Power.text: Link 4: Power. The position in the chain that holds the capacity to reorganise last-mile flows, and so to supply binding: mainly the shipper's, the receiver's and the city's.

GL-Link_5_The_holder.speaker: marigold
GL-Link_5_The_holder.text: Link 5: The holder. Who controls the point where the parties' parcels, data or customers meet, and whether it sells delivery to those customers.

GL-Holder_classes.speaker: marigold
GL-Holder_classes.text: Holder classes. Receiver, no-stake third party, helper, public body, rival party or joint holder.

GL-Helper.speaker: marigold
GL-Helper.text: Helper. An operator hired to work for a holder.

GL-Wall.speaker: marigold
GL-Wall.text: Wall. Something that keeps the parties apart.

GL-Penalty.speaker: marigold
GL-Penalty.text: Penalty. A cost a party bears if it stays out.

GL-Thin_flows.speaker: marigold
GL-Thin_flows.text: Thin flows. A low volume of freight between the parties.

GL-Reciprocal_hostage.speaker: marigold
GL-Reciprocal_hostage.text: Reciprocal hostage. An arrangement in which each party holds something of the other's (its parcels, its volumes or its access to a market) that it would forfeit by defecting; Williamson's term.

GL-Gain_share.speaker: marigold
GL-Gain_share.text: Gain-share. A contract that divides the saving a collaboration produces by a formula agreed in advance.

GL-The_condition_S_P_L_W_.speaker: marigold
GL-The_condition_S_P_L_W_.text: The condition (S + P ≥ L + W). Rivals pool only when the saving (S) plus any penalty for staying out (P) covers the exposure of their customers, brand or data (L) plus the cost of the wall that stops it (W): the first finding written as an inequality.

GL-The_overlap_paradox.speaker: marigold
GL-The_overlap_paradox.text: The overlap paradox. The pairs with most to save are the ones who refuse, because where the saving peaks, the exposure peaks with it.

GL-The_holder_principle.speaker: marigold
GL-The_holder_principle.text: The holder principle. That the holder decides how much of a carrier's exposure is at stake.

GL-The_display.speaker: marigold
GL-The_display.text: The display. The visibility of its own brand that a carrier gives up at a shared point, whoever holds it.

GL-Exposure_term.speaker: marigold
GL-Exposure_term.text: Exposure term. The measure of what a holder can expose.

GL-The_red_cell_rule.speaker: marigold
GL-The_red_cell_rule.text: The red-cell rule. A shared parcel point should be held by a party with no stake in the customers of the carriers it serves, and looked at again whenever control of it changes, beside an access rule by vehicle and hour that names no operator.

GL-Access_rule_by_vehicle_and_hour_rule_.speaker: marigold
GL-Access_rule_by_vehicle_and_hour_rule_.text: Access rule by vehicle and hour (rule by vehicle and hour). A rule on which vehicles may enter at which hours, applying to every company alike; it names no operator, and survives as the penalty P.

GL-The_dot.speaker: marigold
GL-The_dot.text: The dot. A sign of a stake, named after the inclusion the spleen removes from a red cell.

GL-Separated_second_version.speaker: marigold
GL-Separated_second_version.text: Separated second version. A separate arm of the carrier run by different people.

GL-Neutral_point_and_open_point.speaker: marigold
GL-Neutral_point_and_open_point.text: Neutral point and open point. A neutral point is held by a party with no stake; an open point is open to any carrier. Council sites are awarded neutral first and open second.

GL-Neutral_orchestrator.speaker: marigold
GL-Neutral_orchestrator.text: Neutral orchestrator. A party that sells neither delivery nor the parties' kind of goods to their customers, the neutral holder of 6.3.

GL-Rule_1a.speaker: marigold
GL-Rule_1a.text: Rule 1a. The codebook rule for the trustee schemes: it codes a trustee that runs a scheme as its holder and the operator it hires as a helper. Added after the results were seen; every result is reported with and without it.

GL-Drift_by_sale.speaker: marigold
GL-Drift_by_sale.text: Drift by sale. A neutral point passing by sale to a holder with a stake.

GL-The_receiver_s_clock.speaker: marigold
GL-The_receiver_s_clock.text: The receiver's clock. The hours when receivers will take goods in; the limit on any rule by hour.

GL-The_visibility_veto.speaker: marigold
GL-The_visibility_veto.text: The visibility veto. A firm refusing to collaborate because its branded vans would no longer be seen.

GL-Mirror_pairs.speaker: marigold
GL-Mirror_pairs.text: Mirror pairs. The cases in which the same firm, or the same kind of firm, said yes and no in the same breath, one answer for each side of the line.

GL-The_substitution.speaker: marigold
GL-The_substitution.text: The substitution. The finding that something outside the parties, and not their trust, binds most of the collaborations in the set.

GL-The_four_pillars.speaker: marigold
GL-The_four_pillars.text: The four pillars. Trust, efficiency, innovation and sustainability: the framework the 2024 fieldwork was designed under, which the data replaced.

GL-The_big_fierce_animal.speaker: marigold
GL-The_big_fierce_animal.text: The big fierce animal. The author's 2022 image, used in his own way and not Colinvaux's: the large carrier stands alone because it takes everything within reach, while small operators share. The data corrected it to overlap; 6.4 keeps it as an image of territory.

GL-The_working_claim_of_2026.speaker: marigold
GL-The_working_claim_of_2026.text: The working claim of 2026. That the last mile is a brand asset, that size sorts willingness, that working arrangements run on substitutes for trust, that the power sits with shippers and cities and that time can do what pooling was asked to. The second coding tested it; brand and size fell.

GL-Stance.speaker: marigold
GL-Stance.text: Stance. Whether a paper or transcript supports a link, contradicts it, is mixed or is silent.

GL-Replication.speaker: marigold
GL-Replication.text: Replication. One of two separately run pairs of coding passes; a result must hold in both.

GL-Running_rows.speaker: marigold
GL-Running_rows.text: Running rows. Arrangements running at interview.

GL-Rivals_not_far_from_the_customer.speaker: marigold
GL-Rivals_not_far_from_the_customer.text: Rivals not far from the customer. Rivals working at the last leg, at the door or at no stage named.

GL-Necessary_condition_in_the_comparativ.speaker: marigold
GL-Necessary_condition_in_the_comparativ.text: Necessary condition (in the comparative analysis). Present in at least nine in ten running rows (a consistency of 0.9).

GL-The_core.speaker: marigold
GL-The_core.text: The core. A split of the gain that no group would gain by leaving; for rivals it is empty wherever overlap costs them more in customers than pooling saves.

GL-Market_commonality_and_resource_simil.speaker: marigold
GL-Market_commonality_and_resource_simil.text: Market commonality and resource similarity. Chen's (1996) two kinds of overlap: how far two firms serve the same customers, and how far they use the same means.

GL-Principal_and_its_absence_among_peers.speaker: marigold
GL-Principal_and_its_absence_among_peers.text: Principal (and its absence among peers). A party in charge to watch the others and impose penalties; rivals of equal standing have none unless someone from outside takes that role.

GL-Trophic_cascade.speaker: marigold
GL-Trophic_cascade.text: Trophic cascade. The ecologists' name for a change at one level of a food web that reorganises the levels beneath it; here the receiver, not the carrier, is the level whose change reorganises the rest.

GL-The_shared_van.speaker: marigold
GL-The_shared_van.text: The shared van. Competitors' parcels on one van from a consolidation centre: the field's remedy, which so rarely arrived.

GL-Bundler.speaker: marigold
GL-Bundler.text: Bundler. An operator that bundles goods flows; the council in the red-cell rule designs none.

GL-Push_and_pull.speaker: marigold
GL-Push_and_pull.text: Push and pull. The push is the access rule by vehicle and hour; the pull is a shared point held by a party with no stake, sited near residents with a checkout default.

GL-Closed_hours.speaker: marigold
GL-Closed_hours.text: Closed hours. In Ghent, the hours when the loading-and-unloading category may not enter.

GL-Card.speaker: marigold
GL-Card.text: Card. The author's reading note on each paper of the review.

CN-H1.speaker: marigold
CN-H1.text: The Viva Hall is open. Go when you're ready. Not before.

CN-H2.speaker: marigold
CN-H2.text: These three could do with another look first.

CN-H3.speaker: marigold
CN-H3.text: From here on, I'll be quiet. The Hall is yours.

CN-NA1.speaker: marigold
CN-NA1.text: Not today. Every answer is still out there, in your own districts. Ride back, and come again.

CN-W1.speaker: marigold
CN-W1.text: The chain lights over the city, the last link hollow: proposed, not found. You can say every link of it.

CN-W3.speaker: marigold
CN-W3.text: Down in the street, rivals still want the same doors.

CN-W5.speaker: marigold
CN-W5.text: And that's the story of Freight City. Goodnight, Doctor.

CN-MJ1.speaker: marigold
CN-MJ1.text: A long list in red ink, a cold cup of tea, and a parcel that will get there.

CN-MJ2.speaker: marigold
CN-MJ2.text: The story isn't finished. One more ride to the Hall, and it could be.

F-finale-pre-viva-cutscene-1.text: Dr Prudence Tally, internal examiner. I know every table by heart.

MT-anonymisation-plain.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-plain.text: Removing or disguising details that would identify participants, and replacing names with codes.

MT-anonymisation-how1.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-how1.text: Participants are identified by codes A1 to A13 and B1 to B13, in the order the transcripts were filed and divided into the two halves read separately in the second and third codings (3.3).

MT-anonymisation-how2.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-how2.text: No participant and no employer is named in any chapter; organisations are described by type; where a participant's own description would identify them, it was made generic in Table 3.4 (3.3).

MT-anonymisation-how3.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-how3.text: Table 3.4 gives the eleven countries as a set, not against each code (3.3).

MT-anonymisation-how4.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-how4.text: A city or public scheme is named only where it is a matter of public record and more than one person could have described it; a role that would narrow to one person was widened (3.3).

MT-anonymisation-how5.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-how5.text: The transcripts were pseudonymised, with names, employers and places replaced by the codes, before the second coding began (3.4).

MT-anonymisation-why.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-why.text: 'These choices follow Saunders, Kitzinger and Kitzinger (2015), who show that anonymising interview data is a set of judgements rather than a procedure, and the judgements made here are stated so that a reader can see what was traded for what' (3.3).

MT-anonymisation-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-anonymisation-analogy.text: Blurring faces and number plates in a street photograph while keeping the street recognisable enough to tell the story.

MV-anonymisation-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-anonymisation-v1.text: How did you protect participants when the sector is small?

MQ-anonymisation-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-anonymisation-q1.text: Whose work does 3.3 cite for treating anonymisation as a set of judgements?

MQ-anonymisation-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-anonymisation-q2.text: How does Table 3.4 give the eleven countries?

MT-binder_initiator_coding-term.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-term.text: Coding the binder and the initiator of each arrangement

MT-binder_initiator_coding-plain.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-plain.text: For each arrangement, recording what held it together (the binder) and who started it (the initiator), as two separate codes.

MT-binder_initiator_coding-how1.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-how1.text: Appendix H was built after the second coding by listing every collaboration a participant described, one row per description (3.4).

MT-binder_initiator_coding-how2.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-how2.text: 'Each row carries one binder and one initiator.' The binder is what, on the participant's account, held the arrangement once formed; a second binder is given in brackets and not counted; 'a party that only made the introduction or a rule that only supplied the occasion is not counted as a binder' (3.4).

MT-binder_initiator_coding-how3.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-how3.text: The initiator is the party the participant said began the arrangement, coded apart from whoever holds it (3.4).

MT-binder_initiator_coding-how4.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-how4.text: The ninety-five rows bound from outside (4.4) rest on the binder; the forty-two rows begun by a city or public body and the nineteen by a carrier (4.5) rest on the initiator (3.4).

MT-binder_initiator_coding-how5.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-how5.text: Both were assigned once, by hand, in building the appendix. 'The binder was not coded a second time, so unlike the codes of October 2026 it carries no agreement figure'; the initiator was re-checked in both passes of October 2026, read the same way in 98 of 117 rows (alpha .80) (3.4; 3.7).

MT-binder_initiator_coding-how6.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-how6.text: The A half's first listing recorded every mechanism a participant named, while the appendix gives one binder per row, so the two tallies differ and 4.4 gives both (3.4).

MT-binder_initiator_coding-why.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-why.text: The thesis says what was done and states the gap as a limit (3.7); it does not say why the binder was not coded a second time.

MT-binder_initiator_coding-analogy.speaker: manny
MT-binder_initiator_coding-analogy.text: For each marriage on a register, noting who proposed and what keeps it going, and keeping the two columns separate.

MV-binder_initiator_coding-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-binder_initiator_coding-v1.text: Your 95 of 117 rests on a code assigned once. How reliable is it?

MV-binder_initiator_coding-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-binder_initiator_coding-v2.text: Why keep the initiator separate from the holder?

MQ-binder_initiator_coding-q1.speaker: manny
MQ-binder_initiator_coding-q1.text: Which of these carries no agreement figure?

MQ-binder_initiator_coding-q2.text: How many of the 117 rows were begun by a city or public body?
