MT-interviewer_effects-how3.text: Relayed positions: the shipper-responsibility thesis relayed to two as something others had said; one participant's case narrated to another; the claim that small operators collaborate hard put to two, who did not take it up (4.1).

MT-interviewer_effects-how4.speaker: sam
MT-interviewer_effects-how4.text: Where a participant took up a seeded theme, as B5 took up the trustee, it is counted with the seeding noted (4.1).

MT-interviewer_effects-how5.speaker: sam
MT-interviewer_effects-how5.text: Five cautions of the second coding are carried into the thesis as written: brand declined in five of five; relayed positions mean agreement across transcripts partly reflects the interviewer; one recording substantially incomplete; one participant's successes were proposals; one case not yet running at interview (3.4).

MT-interviewer_effects-why.speaker: sam
MT-interviewer_effects-why.text: The interviewer 'is the reader most exposed to his own expectation, which Miles, Huberman and Saldaña name among the first threats to a qualitative analysis' (3.4). Recording seeded and relayed themes is part of reflexivity (3.7).

MT-interviewer_effects-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-interviewer_effects-analogy.text: A detective noting which details he mentioned to a witness first, so a later 'match' with his own theory isn't mistaken for corroboration.

MV-interviewer_effects-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-interviewer_effects-v1.text: You raised brand yourself. How did you stop that colouring the result?

MV-interviewer_effects-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-interviewer_effects-v2.text: You relayed one participant's views to another. Doesn't that make agreement across transcripts partly your doing?

MQ-interviewer_effects-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-interviewer_effects-q1.text: How is brand counted, given the interviewer raised it?

MQ-interviewer_effects-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-interviewer_effects-q2.text: Which of these is one of the five cautions of the second coding?

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-term.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-term.text: Item-level denominators and the skip that was not applied

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-plain.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-plain.text: When respondents skip questions, each question is reported out of those who answered it. A 'skip' is a rule that sends some respondents past questions not meant for them; if it fails, unintended people answer.

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how1.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how1.text: Of 132 responses, six answered No to consent and seven gave consent but nothing more; the other 119 are usable, 'and every one of them is kept, however many items it answered. Each item is reported of those who answered it, with that number beside it' (3.6).

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how2.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how2.text: 'The form did not apply the draft's skip, and the answers are reported as they stand' (3.6).

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how3.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how3.text: 36 of the 109 who answered said they collaborate now, but 48 said how long they had been involved (12 of them had answered No) and 48 rated their collaboration's success (36 collaborating now, 12 not); these are 'read as past engagement' (3.6).

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how4.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how4.text: Goals were answered by 107, 68 of them not collaborating now, read as goals a company has or would have; mechanisms of trust by 45 (11 not now), benefits by 49 (13), challenges by 93 (53), read as past or expected collaboration (3.6).

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how5.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how5.text: 'A challenge named by a company that does not collaborate now may be one it met in an earlier attempt or one it expects, and the item cannot tell the two apart' (3.6).

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how6.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-how6.text: The duration answers run from '1-3 years' to 'More than 5 years', with nothing between; the draft had offered 'More than 3 years' (3.6).

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-why.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-why.text: The thesis keeps every usable response and reports each item against those who answered (3.6). It does not say why the skip was not applied; it names it among the irregularities a pilot might have caught.

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-not.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-not.text: Dropping partial responses, or forcing the draft's skip after the fact; neither is done.

MT-item_denominators_and_skip-analogy.speaker: lockie
MT-item_denominators_and_skip-analogy.text: A form that says 'married people only, answer section C', but has no gate: you count section C out of whoever filled it in, and say who they were.

MV-item_denominators_and_skip-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-item_denominators_and_skip-v1.text: Twelve companies that don't collaborate rated their collaboration's success. How do you read that?

MV-item_denominators_and_skip-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-item_denominators_and_skip-v2.text: Why does each survey item have a different denominator?

MQ-item_denominators_and_skip-q1.speaker: lockie
MQ-item_denominators_and_skip-q1.text: Of the 48 who rated their collaboration's success, how many said they do not collaborate now?

MQ-item_denominators_and_skip-q2.speaker: lockie
MQ-item_denominators_and_skip-q2.text: What gap does the duration item have?

MG-item_denominators_and_skip.speaker: lockie
MG-item_denominators_and_skip.text: Why the skip was not applied is not stated.

MT-krippendorff_alpha-plain.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-plain.text: A measure of how far two codings agree beyond what chance alone would produce. 1 means perfect agreement; 0 means no better than chance.

MT-krippendorff_alpha-how1.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-how1.text: Used for the 117 arrangements 'because there the unit is the arrangement, the cases number 117 and the codes are nominal', against Krippendorff's bar of '.800 for firm conclusions and .667 for tentative ones (2004, p. 241)' (3.4).

MT-krippendorff_alpha-how2.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-how2.text: Codebook version 2: market commonality .84, footprint .84, outcome .87 (firm); the wall .76 (tentative); the penalty .54 over all 117, though the passes never disagree on it among rivals not far from the customer; stage of the chain .59, volume of flows .55, what crosses .65 (below the tentative bar) (3.4).

MT-krippendorff_alpha-how3.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-how3.text: Version 3: holder's class .88; rivalry among co-users .85; whether the holder sells delivery .87 over all 117, 'partly built in because rival and joint holders sell by definition', and .72 (tentative) on the helper rows; the derived neutral holder .84 (3.4).

MT-krippendorff_alpha-how4.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-how4.text: The initiator, re-checked in both passes of October 2026: 98 of 117 rows, alpha .80 (3.4).

MT-krippendorff_alpha-how5.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-how5.text: Elsewhere: the re-run of the 2023 full-text stage, thirty of thirty-one on subject, alpha .91 (3.2); the locker owners, .87 on class and .81 on neutral against rival-held, over forty-seven ownership periods (3.5).

MT-krippendorff_alpha-why.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-why.text: Unit is the arrangement, 117 cases, nominal codes (3.4).

MT-krippendorff_alpha-not.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-not.text: Raw agreement, used for the transcripts (3.4); Cohen's kappa, used for the survey's open answers (3.6).

MT-krippendorff_alpha-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-krippendorff_alpha-analogy.text: Two people guessing coin tosses will agree half the time by luck; alpha only gives credit for agreement beyond that luck.

MX-krippendorff_alpha-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-krippendorff_alpha-b1.text: Two codings agree. But how much of that agreement is luck?

MX-krippendorff_alpha-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-krippendorff_alpha-b2.text: Even random guesses match sometimes, like two coin tosses landing the same.

MX-krippendorff_alpha-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-krippendorff_alpha-b3.text: Krippendorff's alpha counts only agreement beyond chance. One is perfect; zero is luck.

MX-krippendorff_alpha-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-krippendorff_alpha-b4.text: Two bars: .667 for tentative conclusions, .800 for firm ones.

MX-krippendorff_alpha-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-krippendorff_alpha-b5.text: The holder's class scored .88. The penalty, .54, and the thesis says so.

MV-krippendorff_alpha-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-krippendorff_alpha-v1.text: Several of your version 2 variables fall below .667. What follows?

MV-krippendorff_alpha-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-krippendorff_alpha-v1-ans.text: I report them as they fell. The penalty is .54 over all 117, though the passes never disagree on it among rivals not far from the customer, the rows that matter; stage of the chain, volume and what crosses fall below too. Every disagreement was listed, the rows where a difference changes a result isolated, and each settled against the codebook with its reason recorded (3.4).

MV-krippendorff_alpha-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-krippendorff_alpha-v2.text: Your 'holder sells delivery' alpha is .87. Isn't that flattered?

MV-krippendorff_alpha-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-krippendorff_alpha-v2-ans.text: Partly, and I say so: it is partly built in because rival and joint holders sell by definition. On the helper rows, where the code carries information, it is .72, tentative (3.4).

MQ-krippendorff_alpha-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-krippendorff_alpha-q1.text: What alpha does Krippendorff set for firm conclusions?

MQ-krippendorff_alpha-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-krippendorff_alpha-q2.text: What was the alpha for the holder's class in codebook version 3?

MQ-krippendorff_alpha-q3.speaker: sal
MQ-krippendorff_alpha-q3.text: Why is alpha used for the arrangements but not the transcripts?

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-term.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-term.text: Other choices made after the results were seen (thin flows; rows where something crosses)

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-plain.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-plain.text: Any analytic choice made after seeing results is a risk of fitting the analysis to the answer; the safeguard is to say so and show the result both ways.

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how1.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how1.text: 'Two other choices in the analysis of the 117 were made after the first results were seen: thin flows (a low volume of freight between the parties) as a condition, added for the rural row (H.1 42), and the restriction to rows where something crosses between the parties; both are reported as such (4.4, Appendix L.4)' (3.7).

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how2.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how2.text: Thin flows: the rural case, offered as an inference, had neither a wall nor a penalty but thin flows, and is counted as running (4.4).

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how3.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how3.text: The restriction: kept to rows where something that would expose customers, brand, data or freight crossed, the contrast is 7 of 8 running with a wall or penalty against 1 of 6 with neither, and 8 of 9 against 1 of 7 (4.4).

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how4.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-how4.text: The main text does not give the reason for the restriction. Appendix L does: it follows from S + P ≥ L + W, since where nothing crosses, L = 0 and no wall is needed; and it was specified after the counting error was found.

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-why.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-why.text: Thin flows was added 'for the rural row (H.1 42)' (3.7). For the restriction, see the gap.

MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-analo.speaker: manny
MT-late_choices_reported_both_ways-analo.text: A surveyor who moves a boundary marker after the first measurements must mark both lines on the map.

MV-late_choices_reported_both_ways-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-late_choices_reported_both_ways-v1.text: Which of your analytic choices came after you saw the results?

MV-late_choices_reported_both_ways-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-late_choices_reported_both_ways-v2.text: Why restrict to rows where something crosses?

MQ-late_choices_reported_both_ways-q1.speaker: manny
MQ-late_choices_reported_both_ways-q1.text: For which row was thin flows added as a condition?

MQ-late_choices_reported_both_ways-q2.speaker: manny
MQ-late_choices_reported_both_ways-q2.text: Kept to rows where something crosses, how many arrangements with neither a wall nor a penalty were running in one replication?

MG-late_choices_reported_both_ways.speaker: manny
MG-late_choices_reported_both_ways.text: The main text does not give the reason for restricting to rows where something crosses; only Appendix L does.

MT-likert_items-plain.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-plain.text: Questions answered on a numbered scale, here 1 to 5, between two labelled ends, such as 'not important' and 'extremely important'.

MT-likert_items-how1.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-how1.text: 'Three items are five-point Likert-type items (Likert, 1932), and they do not run the same way' (3.6).

MT-likert_items-how2.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-how2.text: Success: 1 very successful to 5 very unsuccessful. Importance of trust: 1 not important to 5 extremely important. Likelihood of more collaboration: 1 very likely to 5 very unlikely (3.6).

MT-likert_items-how3.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-how3.text: 'Every table that reports them states the direction' (3.6).

MT-likert_items-how4.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-how4.text: The draft's worded scales for success and future engagement became scales of 1 to 5 in the final form (3.6).

MT-likert_items-how5.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-how5.text: Results are reported as counts and percentages, e.g. trust: 68 chose 5 and 21 chose 4, 89 of 119 (75 per cent), none chose 1 or 2 (5.3).

MT-likert_items-why.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-why.text: The thesis states the items and directions; it does not say why the directions differ.

MT-likert_items-analogy.speaker: lockie
MT-likert_items-analogy.text: Three thermometers, two marked hot at the top and one hot at the bottom: readable, provided every reading says which way up it was.

MV-likert_items-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-likert_items-v1.text: Your three scales run in different directions. Did that cause errors?

MV-likert_items-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-likert_items-v2.text: How did you summarise the Likert answers?

MQ-likert_items-q1.speaker: lockie
MQ-likert_items-q1.text: On the trust item, what does 5 mean?

MQ-likert_items-q2.speaker: lockie
MQ-likert_items-q2.text: On the likelihood item, what does 1 mean?

MG-likert_items.speaker: lockie
MG-likert_items.text: Why the scales run in different directions, and whether that confused respondents, is not discussed.

MT-limitations_and_critique-term.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-term.text: Limitations and the critique with hindsight

MT-limitations_and_critique-plain.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-plain.text: An honest list of what the research could not show, with the consequence of each, and what a critic would say with hindsight.

MT-limitations_and_critique-how1.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-how1.text: The paradigm's cost: 'a mechanism named from twenty-six accounts is retroduced and not observed, so it is a proposition, and it generalises to the mechanism and not to a population' (3.7).

MT-limitations_and_critique-how2.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-how2.text: Carriers: four of twenty-six interviews speak for a carrier (three of thirty voices, a fourth an adviser to one); much of what is said of carriers is second-hand, though from people who negotiated with them for years (3.7; 7.4).

MT-limitations_and_critique-how3.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-how3.text: Out-of-domain transcripts kept in every denominator; the binder assigned once, with no agreement figure; silence counts may be too high; the survey self-selected, unpiloted and on the pillars (3.7).

MT-limitations_and_critique-how4.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-how4.text: Ghent read in documents, not its operators or permit register (3.7; 7.4).

MT-limitations_and_critique-how5.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-how5.text: Fifth link: coded by holder class, not pair by pair; 26 ownership periods; much of carriers' use known from regulators and the press; support only under rule 1a; thin flows and the restriction chosen after results; networks not matched on quality; drift by sale rests on two changes of owner, each read both ways; the scenario a worked example; no residents, shopkeepers or employed drivers interviewed; no court has ruled on the rule's proportionality (3.7).

MT-limitations_and_critique-how6.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-how6.text: Translations not checked by a Dutch speaker (7.4).

MT-limitations_and_critique-how7.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-how7.text: Critique with hindsight: a positivist design would have measured what was counted and said less about why; an interpretivist one would have said nothing about the mechanism; 'a guide written after the fact would have asked about overlap and time directly and found less than it was told, because the participants brought both unprompted' (7.4).

MT-limitations_and_critique-why.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-why.text: The thesis states them with their consequences ('One further limit is stated with its consequence', 7.4); it gives no separate reason for the section.

MT-limitations_and_critique-analogy.speaker: nora
MT-limitations_and_critique-analogy.text: A surveyor's report that marks on the map which areas were measured on foot and which were sketched from a distance.

MV-limitations_and_critique-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-limitations_and_critique-v1.text: What would a critic say with hindsight?

MV-limitations_and_critique-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-limitations_and_critique-v1-ans.text: That a positivist design would have measured overlap against willingness across a sample and said less about why; that an interpretivist one would have said nothing about the mechanism; and that the fieldwork was designed under a framework the data replaced. Against the last, a guide written after the fact would have found less, because participants brought overlap and time unprompted (7.4).

MV-limitations_and_critique-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-limitations_and_critique-v2.text: What does your argument need that you did not observe directly?

MV-limitations_and_critique-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-limitations_and_critique-v2-ans.text: The receiver's clock, which I read in participants' accounts and Ghent's actor table, with no shopkeeper interviewed; and the rule by vehicle and hour in practice, read in Ghent's documents, not its operators or permit register. Both are further studies (3.5; 7.4; 7.5).

MQ-limitations_and_critique-q1.speaker: nora
MQ-limitations_and_critique-q1.text: How many of the thirty voices are carriers', according to 7.4?

MQ-limitations_and_critique-q2.speaker: nora
MQ-limitations_and_critique-q2.text: Which groups were not interviewed at all?

MT-locker_networks_sample-term.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-term.text: The locker networks: inclusion rule, ownership periods and the main-carrier denominator

MT-locker_networks_sample-plain.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-plain.text: How the set of parcel-locker networks was chosen and what was counted in each, so the comparison by owner can be repeated.

MT-locker_networks_sample-how1.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-how1.text: Inclusion: 'A network of parcel lockers or staffed pick-up points in Europe or the United Kingdom was included where its owner can be identified and at least one source says which carriers deliver into it, or that it is closed to all but its owner' (3.5).

MT-locker_networks_sample-how2.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-how2.text: Result: forty-three networks in sixteen countries; forty-seven ownership periods 'once a network sold during the evidence window is counted once for each owner'; 210 rows of evidence on which carrier delivers where, 'with each country's main carriers as the denominator' (3.5).

MT-locker_networks_sample-how3.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-how3.text: Each owner coded twice, independently, as neutral or by the kind of rival holding it: alpha .87 on class, .81 on neutral against rival-held, over forty-seven ownership periods (3.5).

MT-locker_networks_sample-how4.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-how4.text: The test uses the twenty-five open networks, 'leaving out each owner's own group': twenty-six ownership periods, twelve neutral-held and fourteen rival-held (3.5; 5.2).

MT-locker_networks_sample-how5.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-how5.text: 'Its rules were written before the run, and the two added once the networks had been listed are stated in Appendix M' (3.5).

MT-locker_networks_sample-how6.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-how6.text: A main carrier for which no source was found is counted as not delivering (5.2).

MT-locker_networks_sample-why.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-why.text: The ownership period is the unit 'so that a network sold during the evidence window counts once for each owner' (3.1). The thesis does not say why each country's main carriers are the denominator.

MT-locker_networks_sample-not.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-not.text: Counting by pair of network and carrier, also reported but not relied on (see Fisher's exact test).

MT-locker_networks_sample-analogy.speaker: lockie
MT-locker_networks_sample-analogy.text: Counting shops by each owner they have had, so a shop sold mid-year appears once under each owner, with each town's main suppliers as the yardstick.

MV-locker_networks_sample-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-locker_networks_sample-v1.text: Why count ownership periods rather than networks?

MV-locker_networks_sample-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-locker_networks_sample-v2.text: A carrier you found no source for is counted as not delivering. Doesn't that bias the result?

MQ-locker_networks_sample-q1.speaker: lockie
MQ-locker_networks_sample-q1.text: How many ownership periods enter the locker test?

MQ-locker_networks_sample-q2.speaker: lockie
MQ-locker_networks_sample-q2.text: What is the denominator for each network's share?

MG-locker_networks_sample.speaker: lockie
MG-locker_networks_sample.text: Why main carriers are the denominator is not argued; how the two rules added after listing affected the run is in Appendix M only.

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-plain.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-plain.text: A regularity is a pattern that recurs across cases. A mechanism is what produces it. Critical realist research names the mechanism and checks it against cases where it should have produced the pattern.

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how1.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how1.text: The regularity: 'a refusal to collaborate that comes back wherever the parties' customers overlap', across twenty-six accounts (3.1).

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how2.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how2.text: The mechanisms named: overlap and binding (3.1).

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how3.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how3.text: What counts as a finding under critical realism: 'A mechanism, named and shown to have operated in the case (Easton, 2010; Wynn and Williams, 2012)' (Table 3.2).

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how4.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how4.text: The mechanism was tested against the cases that should break it: 'the one city that already shares out delivery hours by law', and the holder against 'the 117 arrangements, forty-three locker networks and the rules that say when a point is neutral' (3.1).

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how5.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-how5.text: How it generalises: 'To the mechanism, not the population; it may fire elsewhere under other conditions (Easton, 2010)' (Table 3.2).

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-why.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-why.text: 'Faced with a pattern that keeps recurring, it does not ask what caused it in one case but what must be true for it to keep happening; the answer is a mechanism, which is then checked against the cases where it should have worked and did not' (3.1; Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992).

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-not.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-not.text: Positivist finding: 'A relationship between variables, stated so it could be falsified'. Interpretivist finding: 'A credible interpretation, thick enough for a reader to recognise the setting' (Table 3.2).

MT-mechanism_and_regularity-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-mechanism_and_regularity-analogy.text: A rash that keeps appearing on the same patients is the regularity; the allergy is the mechanism; the doctor then checks patients who ate the food and had no rash.

MV-mechanism_and_regularity-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-mechanism_and_regularity-v1.text: What is the regularity, and what is the mechanism?

MV-mechanism_and_regularity-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-mechanism_and_regularity-v2.text: Your propositions each relate two variables. Isn't that positivist?

MQ-mechanism_and_regularity-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-mechanism_and_regularity-q1.text: Under critical realism, what counts as a finding (Table 3.2)?

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-term.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-term.text: Borrowed concepts: ecology as theory, the red cell as a labelled design guide

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-plain.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-plain.text: Concepts from another field can be used as a source of ideas, provided their fit is argued and no empirical claim rests on the borrowed image itself.

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how1.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how1.text: Ecology is 'read as a source of concepts rather than of evidence, in the manner Benyus (1997) proposed', with weight carried by Gause (1934), Hardin (1960), Schoener (1974), Carothers and Jaksić (1984) and Kronfeld-Schor and Dayan (2003) (2.6).

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how2.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how2.text: 'The biology is used as Cornelissen (2005) says a metaphor should be used in organisational theory: as a source of concepts whose fit is argued and tested, with every empirical claim carried by the ecology papers and the interviews, never by the image' (2.6).

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how3.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how3.text: The red cell is 'used here as a labelled design guide, not as theory' (2.6); 'The ecology of Chapter 2 is a theoretical perspective, openly declared and held to the same standard as the others. The red cell of 6.3 is an analogy used as a design guide, and the thesis says so' (1.6).

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how4.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-how4.text: Limits are carried: Gause's tube held creatures that could not choose; Hardin wrote 'we still do not comprehend the exact limits of the principle'; birds' red cells keep their nucleus (Stier et al., 2013), 'so neutrality is a reading of the biology, not its law'; the spleen holds no hearing; inclusions are a poor measure of spleen function (de Porto et al., 2010) (2.6).

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-why.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-why.text: Cornelissen's account of metaphor (2.6), and 'it uses an image where an image makes an argument better than a definition would' (1.6).

MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-metaphor_and_design_guide-analogy.text: An architect borrowing the honeycomb: it suggests a strong shape, but the engineer still has to calculate the loads.

MV-metaphor_and_design_guide-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-metaphor_and_design_guide-v1.text: What is the difference between your ecology and your red cell?

MV-metaphor_and_design_guide-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-metaphor_and_design_guide-v2.text: How do you stop a metaphor doing work it shouldn't?

MQ-metaphor_and_design_guide-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-metaphor_and_design_guide-q1.text: Whose account of metaphor in organisational theory does 2.6 follow?

MQ-metaphor_and_design_guide-q2.speaker: ada
MQ-metaphor_and_design_guide-q2.text: What status does the thesis give the red cell?

MT-necessary_condition_bar-term.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-term.text: Necessary conditions, consistency and the 0.9 bar

MT-necessary_condition_bar-plain.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-plain.text: A necessary condition is one that is present whenever the outcome occurs. Consistency is the share of outcome cases that have it; the thesis treats 0.9 (nine in ten) as the bar.

MT-necessary_condition_bar-how1.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-how1.text: A condition is taken as necessary 'at 0.9 (present in at least nine in ten running rows), below which it is reported as present in most running rows' (3.4).

MT-necessary_condition_bar-how2.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-how2.text: Version 2 (wall includes a trustee or a helper's position): a wall, a penalty or thin flows in 12 of 15 and 12 of 14 running rows, below the bar (4.4).

MT-necessary_condition_bar-how3.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-how3.text: Version 3 (wall narrowed to data separation, contracts, white labels and physical separation; holder coded on its own): wall, penalty or thin flows in 6 of 10 running rows with a holder code, in both replications (4.4).

MT-necessary_condition_bar-how4.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-how4.text: Adding a holder with no stake in the parties' customers: 9 of 10, 'which meets the bar' (4.4).

MT-necessary_condition_bar-how5.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-how5.text: Without rule 1a the three trustee rows drop out and necessity is 6 of 7, with or without the holder, below the bar (4.4; 1.5).

MT-necessary_condition_bar-how6.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-how6.text: Hence 'the interviews support the holder only under that rule' (4.4; 6.5).

MT-necessary_condition_bar-why.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-why.text: 0.9 is given as the conventional threshold (Schneider and Wagemann, 2012) (3.4); no further reason is given.

MT-necessary_condition_bar-not.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-not.text: Sufficiency, the other QCA relation, taken at 0.8 (3.4).

MT-necessary_condition_bar-analogy.speaker: manny
MT-necessary_condition_bar-analogy.text: If nine of every ten houses that survived a flood had raised floors, raised floors look necessary; if only six of seven did, you can't say that with the same confidence.

MX-necessary_condition_bar-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-necessary_condition_bar-b1.text: A necessary condition is one present wherever the outcome is.

MX-necessary_condition_bar-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-necessary_condition_bar-b2.text: The bar used here is 0.9: present in nine of every ten running rows.

MX-necessary_condition_bar-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-necessary_condition_bar-b3.text: Wall, penalty, thin flows, or a holder with no stake: nine of ten. Met.

MX-necessary_condition_bar-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-necessary_condition_bar-b4.text: But that needs rule 1a, added late. Without it: six of seven.

MX-necessary_condition_bar-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-necessary_condition_bar-b5.text: So the thesis reports both, and calls the holder a proposition.

MV-necessary_condition_bar-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-necessary_condition_bar-v1.text: Nine of ten is exactly on the bar. Isn't that fragile?

MV-necessary_condition_bar-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-necessary_condition_bar-v1-ans.text: It meets the bar under rule 1a, and I say plainly that the interviews support the holder only under that rule; without it, it is six of seven, below the bar. That's why the holder is a proposition, not a finding, and why every result is given both ways (4.4; 6.5). Appendix L also shows that dropping each case in turn, the necessity figure ranges from 0.89 to 1.00, lowest without one of the trustee rows.

MV-necessary_condition_bar-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-necessary_condition_bar-v2.text: What is the condition whose necessity you test?

MV-necessary_condition_bar-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-necessary_condition_bar-v2-ans.text: Among rivals not far from the customer, that a running arrangement has a wall, a penalty, thin flows, or a holder with no stake in their customers. With the holder added, under rule 1a, it is present in nine of ten running rows (4.4; 1.5).

MQ-necessary_condition_bar-q1.speaker: manny
MQ-necessary_condition_bar-q1.text: At what consistency is a condition reported as necessary?

MQ-necessary_condition_bar-q2.speaker: manny
MQ-necessary_condition_bar-q2.text: Without rule 1a, what is the necessity count?

MG-necessary_condition_bar.speaker: manny
MG-necessary_condition_bar.text: The main text says each case was dropped in turn but not what that showed. Appendix L: necessity ranges 0.89 to 1.00, lowest without H1-11, one of the three trustee rows. An examiner reading Appendix L may raise it.

MT-negative_case_analysis-plain.speaker: sam
MT-negative_case_analysis-plain.text: Deliberately looking for, and recording, the cases that go against your emerging explanation, rather than only the ones that fit.

MT-negative_case_analysis-how1.speaker: sam
MT-negative_case_analysis-how1.text: The second coding 'was required to record, for every clause of it and every transcript, a stance, the exact words and their place in the transcript, and the evidence against as well as for, which is the negative case analysis Lincoln and Guba (1985) ask of a qualitative reading, built into the coding protocol rather than left to the reader's conscience' (3.4).

MT-negative_case_analysis-how2.speaker: sam
MT-negative_case_analysis-how2.text: 'Disconfirming evidence was required of both codings, so that the counts in Chapter 4 report what cut against the chain ... as well as what supported it' (3.7).

MT-negative_case_analysis-how3.speaker: sam
MT-negative_case_analysis-how3.text: Under critical realism 'the interviews were searched as carefully for evidence against the mechanism as for evidence for it' (3.1).

MT-negative_case_analysis-how4.speaker: sam
MT-negative_case_analysis-how4.text: Examples reported: three accounts that cut against the substitution (B11, A2, B9) set out in 4.4; one transcript contradicting overlap, from outside the last mile (7.1); brand counted as declined (3.4).

MT-negative_case_analysis-why.speaker: sam
MT-negative_case_analysis-why.text: It is what Lincoln and Guba ask of a qualitative reading (3.4) and what retroduction needs: a mechanism 'tested against the cases that should break it' (3.1).

MT-negative_case_analysis-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-negative_case_analysis-analogy.text: A building inspector who must sign off a list of every crack found, not just a certificate that the walls look fine.

MV-negative_case_analysis-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-negative_case_analysis-v1.text: How did you make sure you looked for evidence against yourself?

MV-negative_case_analysis-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-negative_case_analysis-v2.text: Name one case that cut against you.

MQ-negative_case_analysis-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-negative_case_analysis-q1.text: Whose call for negative case analysis does 3.4 cite?

MQ-negative_case_analysis-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-negative_case_analysis-q2.text: Where was negative case analysis built in?

MT-next_designs-term.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-term.text: The designs left for further research

MT-next_designs-plain.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-plain.text: The studies that would test what this thesis could only propose, each with its data, its unit and its comparison.

MT-next_designs-how1.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how1.text: 'Seven studies follow from what this thesis could not do, and each is named where the thesis met its limit, with the data it needs, the unit it would count and the comparison it would make' (7.5).

MT-next_designs-how2.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how2.text: 1, measure the physical signal: shippers' carrier choices; unit the award of a contract; branded against unbranded at the same price and time.

MT-next_designs-how3.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how3.text: 2, count the handover: time-stamped delivery records; unit the delivery; a no-stake point against the door or a rival-held point on the same streets.

MT-next_designs-how4.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how4.text: 3, publish the record Ghent's plans do not report: permit and camera counts; unit the cell of a window and a class of operator; before and after a rule by vehicle and hour.

MT-next_designs-how5.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how5.text: 4, the shipper side as a category: the rows of Appendix H and the thirteen papers; unit the arrangement; shipper-begun against carrier-begun.

MT-next_designs-how6.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how6.text: 5, ask the receivers: unit the opening hour; the hour offered against the hour moved.

MT-next_designs-how7.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how7.text: 6, ask whether hours set by a city are acceptable to those they would bind: unit the organisation; a rule by vehicle and hour against hours by class of operator and against no rule.

MT-next_designs-how8.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how8.text: 7, test the propositions as hypotheses 'in a deductive design in a market this thesis did not sample': a survey of operator pairs; unit the pair; each proposition against its falsifier.

MT-next_designs-how9.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-how9.text: For the fifth link: vignettes for planners; use per point against volume; council test parcels for the dot; matched streets before and after (Angrist and Pischke, 2009) from first-attempt records and residents' diaries; re-reading the locker networks after the myflexbox sale with quality, price and terms matched; and applying rule 1a as it stands to arrangements not coded here (7.5).

MT-next_designs-why.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-why.text: Each is 'named where the thesis met its limit' (7.5).

MT-next_designs-analogy.speaker: nora
MT-next_designs-analogy.text: A builder's handover note listing which walls were load-tested and how the next team should test the rest.

MV-next_designs-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-next_designs-v1.text: How would you show that a neutral holder causes carriers to join?

MV-next_designs-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-next_designs-v2.text: How would P1 be tested properly?

MQ-next_designs-q1.speaker: nora
MQ-next_designs-q1.text: What unit would the seventh further study count?

MQ-next_designs-q2.speaker: nora
MQ-next_designs-q2.text: For which design does 7.5 cite Angrist and Pischke (2009)?

MT-non_probability_sample-plain.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-plain.text: A sample in which people chose to respond after seeing a link, rather than being drawn at random from a known list. It cannot represent a wider population, and no response rate can be calculated.

MT-non_probability_sample-how1.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-how1.text: Population: organisations in urban logistics of the kinds 1.1 admits; 'No register of them exists and none was drawn on' (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-how2.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-how2.text: The link was shared on LinkedIn; by email to industry contacts; with the interview participants and through them their networks; through GREEN-LOG and other project networks; on the Universities' Transport Study Group email list; at events; and with research contacts (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-how3.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-how3.text: 'The respondents are therefore a non-probability sample that selected itself', with the referral-chain bias Biernacki and Waldorf (1981) name (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-how4.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-how4.text: Some respondents may be among the thirty interviewed; the form asked for no name, so the overlap cannot be counted, and 'the survey is not a sample independent of the interviews' (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-how5.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-how5.text: 'No response rate can be computed, since no one knows how many saw the link, and none is claimed' (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-how6.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-how6.text: The questionnaire did not ask for a country; four open answers were in Spanish, French, German and Italian; the eleven countries are not claimed for the respondents (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-why.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-why.text: The thesis does not give a reason for distributing this way; it states the consequences (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-not.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-not.text: A probability sample from a register, impossible because no register exists (3.6).

MT-non_probability_sample-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-non_probability_sample-analogy.text: A suggestion box at a conference: useful to hear what people say, but you can't tell how many walked past without writing anything.

MV-non_probability_sample-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-non_probability_sample-v2.text: Could your survey respondents include your interviewees?

MQ-non_probability_sample-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-non_probability_sample-q1.text: Why can no response rate be computed?

MQ-non_probability_sample-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-non_probability_sample-q2.text: Which of these did the questionnaire NOT ask for?

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-ter.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-ter.text: Online interviews, automatic transcripts and quotation conventions

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-pla.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-pla.text: How the conversations were held, recorded and turned into text, and the rules for quoting from that text.

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.text: Held online between July and September 2024, all twenty-six conducted by the author in English; recorded on the call, twenty-four with video and two as audio (3.3).

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.text: Eight to seventy-four minutes; twenty hours and five minutes in all; median forty-three; 146,778 words of speech, appended summaries excluded (3.3).

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.text: Transcripts were made automatically from the recordings and prepared as McLellan, MacQueen and Neidig (2003) advise: kept as made, appended summaries removed, timestamps retained, so the minute and second of every quotation in Chapters 4 and 5 can be found in Appendix H or I (3.3).

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.text: Quotation rules: British spelling; a repeated word and a filler such as 'yeah' removed without marking; every other omission marked with an ellipsis; square brackets either replace an identifying name, place, employer or time of day, or restore a garbled word where its sense was plain, the passage being left unquoted where it was not (3.3).

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.text: In one interview, A9, answers were typed in afterwards rather than transcribed, and it is read as low confidence throughout (3.3; Table 4.1).

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-how.text: Every quotation was checked by the author against its transcript before it was used (3.3). 'One flag runs through all twenty-six: the transcripts are automatic' (4.1).

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-why.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-why.text: Online 'because the participants sat in eleven countries, and the video call has been found to serve qualitative interviewing well where distance would otherwise exclude the people the question needs (Archibald et al., 2019; Lobe, Morgan and Hoffman, 2020)' (3.3).

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-not.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-not.text: Face-to-face interviews are implied but not named; 3.3 notes 'a call is easier to end than a visit'.

MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-ana.speaker: sam
MT-online_interviews_and_transcripts-ana.text: A court stenographer's record with timestamps: anyone can go to the exact minute a quoted line was spoken.

MV-online_interviews_and_transcripts-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-online_interviews_and_transcripts-v1.text: Your transcripts are automatic. How do you know the quotations are right?

MV-online_interviews_and_transcripts-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-online_interviews_and_transcripts-v2.text: Did interviewing online cost you anything?

MQ-online_interviews_and_transcripts-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-online_interviews_and_transcripts-q1.text: What was the total speech in the twenty-six transcripts?

MQ-online_interviews_and_transcripts-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-online_interviews_and_transcripts-q2.text: Which transcript is read as low confidence throughout because answers were typed in afterwards?

MT-openalex-plain.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-plain.text: OpenAlex is a free, open index of scholarly papers. Using it means anyone can re-run the same search without a library subscription.

MT-openalex-how1.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-how1.text: 'One index replaced four databases, because OpenAlex's title-and-abstract field is the nearest single equivalent of the four and can be re-run by anyone with the strings in Appendix E' (3.2).

MT-openalex-how2.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-how2.text: Grounds (3.2): Gusenbauer and Haddaway (2020) separate criteria that 'should always be met by search systems' from those a review may add; the one this review could not do without was that a reader be able to run the search again, which a public index through a public interface meets for any reader and four databases behind institutional logins meet only for subscribers.

MT-openalex-how3.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-how3.text: OpenAlex replaced the Microsoft Academic Graph on its retirement in 2022, 'a fully-open (100% open data, open API, open-source code) source of scholarly metadata' (Priem, Piwowar and Orr, 2022, p. 1) (3.2).

MT-openalex-how4.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-how4.text: On 16.8 million recent publications common to the three, it 'has average source reference numbers and internal coverage rates comparable to both Web of Science and Scopus' (Culbert et al., 2025, p. 2475), while carrying fewer abstracts per article, so every doubtful record was given a second pass with its abstract fetched (3.2).

MT-openalex-how5.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-how5.text: The cost: counts are 'comparable in kind only as far as the title-and-abstract stage' (3.2).

MT-openalex-why.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-why.text: As above: reproducibility for any reader (Gusenbauer and Haddaway, 2020), openness (Priem et al., 2022) and comparable coverage (Culbert et al., 2025) (3.2).

MT-openalex-not.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-not.text: The four subscription databases of 2023: ScienceDirect, Scopus, Web of Science and TRID (Table 3.3).

MT-openalex-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-openalex-analogy.text: Publishing a recipe that uses supermarket ingredients rather than a private supplier's: anyone can cook it again and check the result.

MV-openalex-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-openalex-v1.text: Isn't one index a weaker search than four databases?

MV-openalex-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-openalex-v1-ans.text: The criterion I couldn't do without was that a reader be able to run the search again, which Gusenbauer and Haddaway class among the criteria any search system for a systematic review must meet. A public index through a public interface meets it for any reader; four databases behind logins meet it only for subscribers. On coverage, Culbert and colleagues found OpenAlex comparable to Web of Science and Scopus; its weakness is fewer abstracts, so every doubtful record got a second pass with its abstract fetched (3.2).

MV-openalex-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-openalex-v2.text: What did you lose by switching?

MV-openalex-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-openalex-v2-ans.text: Comparability beyond title and abstract. The forty-nine are papers included after full reading; the 241 were retained after title-and-abstract screening and the citation rule, 170 of them read in full. Wherever the two figures stand together I say which kind each is (3.2).

MQ-openalex-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-openalex-q1.text: What criterion did 3.2 say this review's search could not do without?

MQ-openalex-q2.speaker: ada
MQ-openalex-q2.text: What weakness of OpenAlex does 3.2 name?

MT-p_value-term.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-term.text: The p value and statistical significance

MT-p_value-plain.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-plain.text: A p value is the probability of seeing a result at least as extreme as the one observed if there were in fact no real difference. A small p means the result would be surprising by chance alone; it does not measure size or cause.

MT-p_value-how1.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-how1.text: Locker test, each ownership period counted once: p = .008 (5.2).

MT-p_value-how2.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-how2.text: Pairs of network and carrier, Fisher's exact test: p < .001 for both counts, 'indicative' because the pairs are not independent (5.2).

MT-p_value-how3.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-how3.text: Same carrier, sign test: by carrier group 7 against 2, 10 equal, p = .18; by national name 10 against 2, 9 equal, p = .039 (5.2).

MT-p_value-how4.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-how4.text: On the group count, 'the difference does not reach significance, so the same-carrier check gives the direction and does not prove it' (5.2).

MT-p_value-how5.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-how5.text: The survey runs 'no test of significance' (3.6).

MT-p_value-why.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-why.text: The thesis reports p values for the locker comparison only, where it has a comparison to test (3.5; 5.2). It does not state the significance level it uses.

MT-p_value-not.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-not.text: Significance tests on the survey (not run, 3.6).

MT-p_value-analogy.speaker: lockie
MT-p_value-analogy.text: A smoke alarm's sensitivity: a reading this high would rarely happen with no fire, but it doesn't tell you how big the fire is or who started it.

MV-p_value-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-p_value-v1.text: Your group sign test gives p = .18. Doesn't that undermine the locker result?

MV-p_value-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-p_value-v1-ans.text: It gives the direction and doesn't prove it, and I say so. By group, seven carriers lean neutral and two rival, ten equal, which doesn't reach significance; by national name it's ten against two, p = .039, but the arms of one group share an owner, so the group count is the stricter. The result I rest on is the permutation test, p = .008 (5.2).

MV-p_value-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-p_value-v2.text: What significance level do you use?

MV-p_value-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-p_value-v2-ans.text: The thesis reports the p values and reads them in words, for instance that .18 'does not reach significance'; it doesn't state a level. And each p is read for what it is: a difference by owner class at one time, not a cause (5.2; 7.4).

MQ-p_value-q1.speaker: lockie
MQ-p_value-q1.text: Which p value comes from the sign test by carrier group?

MQ-p_value-q2.speaker: lockie
MQ-p_value-q2.text: What does the thesis conclude from the same-carrier sign tests?

MG-p_value.speaker: lockie
MG-p_value.text: No significance level is stated anywhere in the thesis.

MT-permutation_test-plain.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-plain.text: A test that asks whether a difference between two groups could be luck, by shuffling the group labels many times and seeing how often a difference as large as the real one turns up.

MT-permutation_test-how1.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-how1.text: The comparison is 'by a permutation test on the twenty-six ownership periods that enter it, each counted once (Agresti, 2013)' (3.5).

MT-permutation_test-how2.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-how2.text: On average 46.0 per cent of a country's main carriers deliver into a network held by a firm that sells no delivery, against 21.3 per cent for rival-held networks; permutation test, p = .008 (5.2).

MT-permutation_test-how3.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-how3.text: 'The permutation test above, which counts each ownership period once, is the result the thesis rests on (Appendix M.3)' (5.2).

MT-permutation_test-how4.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-how4.text: Appendix M gives the detail: a difference of 24.7 points, two-sided, 200,000 relabellings.

MT-permutation_test-how5.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-how5.text: 'With so few periods no regression was run' (3.5).

MT-permutation_test-how6.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-how6.text: The result 'is a difference between types of owner. It fits the link but does not test it' (1.5).

MT-permutation_test-why.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-why.text: It 'counts each ownership period once' (5.2), whereas the pair-level counts are not independent; and with so few periods no regression was run (3.5).

MT-permutation_test-not.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-not.text: Fisher's exact test on pairs (reported as indicative) and regression (not run) (3.5; 5.2).

MT-permutation_test-analogy.speaker: lockie
MT-permutation_test-analogy.text: If twelve red and fourteen blue raffle tickets were drawn, and reds won much more often, you'd reshuffle the colours many times and see how often reds win that much by chance.

MX-permutation_test-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-permutation_test-b1.text: Twenty-six ownership periods of locker networks: twelve neutral-held, fourteen rival-held.

MX-permutation_test-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-permutation_test-b2.text: Neutral-held reach 46 per cent of main carriers on average; rival-held, 21.

MX-permutation_test-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-permutation_test-b3.text: Could that gap be luck? Shuffle the colour labels and look again.

MX-permutation_test-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-permutation_test-b4.text: Each shuffle gives a new gap. Repeat it two hundred thousand times.

MX-permutation_test-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-permutation_test-b5.text: Gaps at least as large, either way, appear in fewer than one shuffle in a hundred.

MX-permutation_test-b6.speaker: marigold
MX-permutation_test-b6.text: A real difference by owner class at one time. Not, on its own, a cause.

MV-permutation_test-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-permutation_test-v1.text: Why a permutation test, not regression?

MV-permutation_test-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-permutation_test-v1-ans.text: With twenty-six ownership periods, too few for regression. The permutation test counts each period once, so it doesn't pretend the many pairs of network and carrier are independent; that's why it is the result I rest on: 46.0 against 21.3 per cent, p = .008 (3.5; 5.2).

MV-permutation_test-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-permutation_test-v2.text: Explain p = .008 here in plain words.

MV-permutation_test-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-permutation_test-v2-ans.text: If who holds a network made no difference, and I shuffled the neutral and rival labels across the twenty-six periods, a gap as large as the real one, in either direction, would turn up fewer than one time in a hundred (5.2; Appendix M).

MV-permutation_test-v3.speaker: dr_tally
MV-permutation_test-v3.text: Does p = .008 show that a neutral holder causes carriers to join?

MV-permutation_test-v3-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-permutation_test-v3-ans.text: No. It is a difference by owner class at one time, consistent with the proposition and not a test of it; the networks weren't matched on price, size or terms, and cause is left to reading the networks again after each change of holder (5.2; 7.4; 7.5).

MQ-permutation_test-q1.speaker: lockie
MQ-permutation_test-q1.text: What does the permutation test count once?

MQ-permutation_test-q2.speaker: lockie
MQ-permutation_test-q2.text: What p value does the locker comparison rest on?

MG-permutation_test.speaker: lockie
MG-permutation_test.text: The main text does not say how many relabellings were run or that the test is two-sided; Appendix M does (200,000; two-sided).

MT-piloting-term.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-term.text: Piloting (what was piloted and what was not)

MT-piloting-plain.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-plain.text: Trying an instrument on a small number of cases first, to find problems before using it in full.

MT-piloting-how1.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-how1.text: Arrangement codebook version 1: 'a pilot on ten rows coded independently twice, in which the two codings raised the same problems and seven changes followed' (3.4).

MT-piloting-how2.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-how2.text: Version 3: 'piloted on the same ten rows, extended by eleven rules' (3.4).

MT-piloting-how3.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-how3.text: The survey: 'It was not piloted' (3.6); 'two irregularities a pilot might have caught are in the record: the skip after the question on present collaboration was not applied, and the durations recorded run from ‘1-3 years’ to ‘More than 5 years’ with nothing between' (3.6).

MT-piloting-how4.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-how4.text: The interview guide: built in the sequence Kallio and colleagues (2016) describe, from prerequisites to a preliminary guide and its complete form, and its final questions approved by the supervisory team (3.3); the thesis does not describe a pilot interview.

MT-piloting-why.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-why.text: The pilots of the codebook found problems that led to changes (3.4). The thesis does not say why the survey was not piloted.

MT-piloting-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-piloting-analogy.text: A dress rehearsal: the codebook had two, the survey went on stage without one, and the programme notes say what went wrong.

MQ-piloting-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-piloting-q1.text: Which instrument was piloted on ten rows?

MQ-piloting-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-piloting-q2.text: What followed the first pilot of the arrangement codebook?

MG-piloting.speaker: sam
MG-piloting.text: Whether the interview guide was piloted is not stated; why the survey was not piloted is not stated.

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-term.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-term.text: Positivism and interpretivism (the two paradigms rejected)

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-plain.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-plain.text: Positivism treats reality as measurable and tests hypotheses against measurement, generalising from a sample to a population. Interpretivism treats reality as constructed in people's meanings and builds understanding from what participants say.

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how1.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how1.text: Table 3.2 gives each position's ontology, epistemology, mode of inference (deduction; induction), what counts as a finding, how findings generalise (statistically; they do not, transferability is the reader's judgement) and the researcher's position (stands outside the research; part of the research tool).

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how2.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how2.text: The interpretivist column follows Guba and Lincoln's constructivism, 'labelled interpretivist here as it commonly is' (3.1).

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how3.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how3.text: Where this thesis sits: positivist 'rejected: no register to draw a sample from and no established measure of willingness to test'; interpretivist 'rejected: overlap and binding are held to be real, not only reported' (Table 3.2).

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how4.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-how4.text: Critique with hindsight (7.4): a positivist design 'would have measured what this thesis counted, the overlap of two operators' markets against their willingness across a sample, and it would have said less about why'; an interpretivist one 'would have read the twenty-six for the meaning of collaboration to each and said nothing about the mechanism'.

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-why.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-why.text: Each fails one of the three reasons for critical realism (3.1): positivism needs a full list of operators to draw a sample from and a tested way to measure willingness to collaborate, and the field has neither; interpretivism would not claim that the markets, customers and binders exist however well or badly a participant describes them.

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-not.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-not.text: These are the alternatives; critical realism was adopted.

MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-positivism_and_interpretivism-analogy.text: Positivism is a census with a tape measure; interpretivism is a collection of life stories; the question needed an investigator who uses the stories to reconstruct what actually happened.

MV-positivism_and_interpretivism-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-positivism_and_interpretivism-v1.text: Could a positivist design have done better?

MV-positivism_and_interpretivism-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-positivism_and_interpretivism-v2.text: Your evidence is participants' accounts. Aren't you really an interpretivist?

MQ-positivism_and_interpretivism-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-positivism_and_interpretivism-q2.text: According to 7.4, what would an interpretivist design have said about the mechanism?

MT-prisma-plain.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-plain.text: PRISMA is a reporting standard for systematic reviews. Its flow diagram shows how many records were found and how many left at each screening stage, like a funnel.

MT-prisma-how1.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-how1.text: 2023 flow (Figure 2.1; Table 3.3): 860 identified, a total that counts the eight hand-added papers twice.

MT-prisma-how2.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-how2.text: 662 after the date rule (the 198 published before 2018 set aside, except the eight kept by hand, which are among the 662).

MT-prisma-how3.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-how3.text: 596 downloaded once unsuitable records, duplicates and unobtainable files were out.

MT-prisma-how4.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-how4.text: 263 relevant on title and abstract; 238 after journal refining (25 removed, from fourteen journals, thirteen with a written reason); 72 judged relevant on reading the 238 and read in full; 49 included.

MT-prisma-how5.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-how5.text: 2026 flow (Figure 2.2; Table 3.3): 1,535 identified; 1,023 of eligible type; 254 relevant on title and abstract (208 at first pass, 46 of 150 doubtful records at a second pass with abstracts); 242 records after the citation rule, 241 papers once one article under two DOIs is counted once.

MT-prisma-how6.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-how6.text: The 241 were carded: 170 from full text, 63 from abstracts, 8 from bibliographic records (Table 3.3).

MT-prisma-how7.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-how7.text: PRISMA 2020 item 16b, which asks a review to cite studies that might appear to meet its criteria and say why each was excluded, is the reason the 2023 full-text stage was re-run (3.2).

MT-prisma-why.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-why.text: The thesis reports to PRISMA 2020 (Page et al., 2021) and does not argue for it as such; its one use of a specific item is 16b, the reason for re-running the 2023 full-text stage (3.2).

MT-prisma-not.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-not.text: The thesis names no alternative reporting standard.

MT-prisma-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-prisma-analogy.text: A stack of quarry sieves: each finer mesh holds back a known amount, and the log records what each layer removed.

MX-prisma-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-prisma-b1.text: A systematic review is a funnel. Every record that goes in is counted out again.

MX-prisma-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-prisma-b2.text: In 2022, one search string returned 860 records.

MX-prisma-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-prisma-b3.text: Each stage removes some: dates and duplicates, titles, journals, then full reading.

MX-prisma-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-prisma-b4.text: Forty-nine studies came out of the narrow end.

MX-prisma-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-prisma-b5.text: In 2026 a second funnel, with better strings: 1,535 in, 241 kept.

MX-prisma-b6.speaker: marigold
MX-prisma-b6.text: PRISMA asks you to show every ring, and why each record fell out.

MV-prisma-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-prisma-v1-ans.text: 860 records, a total that counts eight hand-added papers twice; 662 after the date rule; 596 once unsuitable records, duplicates and unobtainable files were out; 263 on title and abstract; 238 after journals whose field lay elsewhere were removed; 72 judged relevant on reading; 49 included after the full texts were read (2.1; Table 3.3).

MV-prisma-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-prisma-v2.text: Your 860 counts eight papers twice. Why report it that way?

MV-prisma-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-prisma-v2-ans.text: Because 860 is the total the 2023 review reported: 662 published from 2018 or kept by hand and 198 from before, with the eight hand-added papers in both. I give its make-up so the reader can see it, and Appendix E sets out the flow as the files support it (2.1; Table 3.3).

MQ-prisma-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-prisma-q1.text: What does PRISMA 2020 item 16b ask a review to do?

MQ-prisma-q2.speaker: ada
MQ-prisma-q2.text: In the 2026 flow, how many records were relevant on title and abstract?

MQ-prisma-q3.speaker: ada
MQ-prisma-q3.text: How many of the 241 update papers were carded from full text?

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-term.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-term.text: Propositions and their falsifiers (P1 to P5, Table 7.1)

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-plain.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-plain.text: A proposition is a single testable statement linking two variables. A falsifier is the observation that would show it wrong.

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how1.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how1.text: Each proposition is 'a single statement relating two variables, under the conditions it names, that others may test in their own context; each is claimed for the mechanism it names, not for a population' (7.2).

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how2.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how2.text: P1: unless a wall, a penalty or an owner with no stake outweighs the exposure, willingness falls as the overlap of customer markets rises. Falsifier: a sample with no wall, penalty or neutral holder in which willingness does not fall with overlap at some size band, or in which size sorts willingness where overlap does not (Table 7.1).

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how3.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how3.text: P2: the more a shared resource constitutes a party's customer relationship, the less likely it is to be pooled. Falsifier: a working arrangement between rivals in the urban last mile pooling freight, customers or operating data with nothing binding it.

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how4.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how4.text: P3: a horizontal collaboration lasts as long as the external arrangement that binds it. Falsifier: an arrangement that outlived its binder on trust alone, or dissolved while its binder stood and its parties still gained.

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how5.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how5.text: P4: an instrument aimed at the party that places the order or writes the permit changes flows more than the same instrument aimed at the carrier. Falsifier: an instrument aimed at carriers that moved flows more.

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how6.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how6.text: P5: at equal access, a carrier's use of a shared point falls as the holder's market commonality with that carrier rises. Falsifier: no difference in use by holder at equal access, or no change in carriers' partner lists after a sale to a rival.

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how7.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-how7.text: Each row of Table 7.1 gives what the proposition rests on and its counts, first and second reading (7.2).

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-why.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-why.text: 'Because the design was theory-building, the contribution is offered as propositions rather than as tested hypotheses' (7.2). A falsifier is 'what a proposition is for' when tested (7.5).

MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-analogy.speaker: nora
MT-propositions_and_falsifiers-analogy.text: A recipe card that also says exactly what result would prove the recipe wrong, so the next cook knows what to look for.

MV-propositions_and_falsifiers-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-propositions_and_falsifiers-v1-ans.text: No difference in carriers' use of a point by holder at equal access, or no change in carriers' lists of partners after a point is sold to a rival (Table 7.1; 2.7).

MV-propositions_and_falsifiers-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-propositions_and_falsifiers-v2.text: Why offer propositions rather than conclusions?

MV-propositions_and_falsifiers-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-propositions_and_falsifiers-v2-ans.text: Because the design was theory-building. Each proposition is a single statement relating two variables, under the conditions it names, claimed for the mechanism and not for a population, with its falsifier, so others can test it in their own context (7.2).

MQ-propositions_and_falsifiers-q1.speaker: nora
MQ-propositions_and_falsifiers-q1.text: Which proposition reads 'The more a shared resource constitutes a party's customer relationship, the less likely it is to be pooled'?

MT-purposive_sampling-plain.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-plain.text: Choosing participants deliberately because they know about the question, rather than at random. The aim is information-rich cases, not a statistically representative sample.

MT-purposive_sampling-how1.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-how1.text: Participants 'were chosen purposively for the kinds of party the question needed (those who run collaborations, those who convene, fund or regulate them, and those who study or broker them), and were found through the projects and publications in which they had done so' (3.3).

MT-purposive_sampling-how2.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-how2.text: 'The sampling was purposeful in Patton's sense (2015), for information-rich cases of each kind of party' (3.3).

MT-purposive_sampling-how3.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-how3.text: The mix: eight public bodies, four consultancies (one a neutral trustee, heard through two staff), six academics (three had worked in industry), four carriers (three from inside one, one the retiring adviser to a small cargo-bike operator; two of the four in one country), and one each for a manufacturing site host, a shipper-side pooling platform, an environmental coalition and a European association of cities (3.3; Table 3.1).

MT-purposive_sampling-how4.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-how4.text: Thirty people in twenty-six interviews: twenty-three with one person, two with a pair, one with three (3.3).

MT-purposive_sampling-how5.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-how5.text: 'Twenty-six is a purposive set, not a sample of a population' (3.3).

MT-purposive_sampling-why.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-why.text: 'The mix was chosen for the question rather than for the industry. If the thing to be explained is who begins a collaboration and what binds it, then the people who convene, fund, regulate, study and broker collaborations had to be in the room, not carriers alone' (3.3).

MT-purposive_sampling-not.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-not.text: A sample of a population (3.3); Table 3.2 notes there is 'no register to draw a sample from'.

MT-purposive_sampling-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-purposive_sampling-analogy.text: To learn why a bridge failed you ask the engineers, inspectors and builders who worked on it, not a random sample of drivers who crossed it.

MV-purposive_sampling-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-purposive_sampling-v1.text: Why not interview mostly carriers, since the thesis is about them?

MV-purposive_sampling-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-purposive_sampling-v1-ans.text: Because the question is who begins a collaboration and what binds it, so the people who convene, fund, regulate, study and broker collaborations had to be in the room, not carriers alone. Carriers, at four voices, are the one kind I call thin, and the others describe carrier behaviour they have watched for years (3.3; 3.7).

MV-purposive_sampling-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-purposive_sampling-v2-ans.text: It isn't meant to be. It's a purposive set chosen for information-rich cases of each kind of party, not a sample of a population, and the findings generalise to the mechanism, not to a population (3.3; 3.1).

MQ-purposive_sampling-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-purposive_sampling-q1.text: Whose sense of purposeful sampling does 3.3 follow?

MQ-purposive_sampling-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-purposive_sampling-q2.text: How many of the twenty-six interviews speak for a public body?

MT-quality_appraisal-plain.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-plain.text: Judging each included study against a checklist of standards (clear question, suitable design, sound analysis) before relying on it.

MT-quality_appraisal-how1.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-how1.text: In the 2023 review, 'the quality appraisal followed the standard quality assessment criteria for primary research papers issued by the Alberta Heritage Foundation for Medical Research's HTA Initiative (Kmet, Lee and Cook, 2004), applied at the full-text stage' (2.1).

MT-quality_appraisal-how2.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-how2.text: At the journal stage, 25 articles from fourteen journals were removed, thirteen of the journals with a written reason (2.1).

MT-quality_appraisal-how3.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-how3.text: The synthesis reads the evidence by kind: of the forty-nine, 12 reviews, 8 frameworks, 16 models, 10 empirical studies, 3 reports; eighteen carry a numerical result of their own, almost all from a model, a simulation or a questionnaire (2.1).

MT-quality_appraisal-how4.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-how4.text: In the update, the cards record what kind each result is: of 116 numerical results, seventy-seven computed from model instances, five carried from elsewhere, thirty-four from empirical studies, and eleven cards measure a running collaboration, seven with an operating figure (2.2).

MT-quality_appraisal-why.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-why.text: The thesis does not say why it chose Kmet, Lee and Cook's criteria, and it does not describe a separate quality appraisal for the 2026 update.

MT-quality_appraisal-not.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-not.text: The thesis names no alternative appraisal tool.

MT-quality_appraisal-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-quality_appraisal-analogy.text: An MOT for papers: each gets the same checklist before it is allowed to carry weight in the argument.

MV-quality_appraisal-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-quality_appraisal-v1.text: How did you appraise the quality of the studies?

MQ-quality_appraisal-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-quality_appraisal-q1.text: Whose criteria did the 2023 quality appraisal follow?

MQ-quality_appraisal-q2.speaker: ada
MQ-quality_appraisal-q2.text: At which stage of the 2023 review was the quality appraisal applied?

MG-quality_appraisal.speaker: ada
MG-quality_appraisal.text: Why Kmet, Lee and Cook, and whether the update appraised quality, are not stated.

MT-quality_criteria-term.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-term.text: Quality in qualitative research: credibility, transferability, dependability, confirmability

MT-quality_criteria-plain.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-plain.text: The qualitative counterparts of validity and reliability: is the account believable (credibility), can a reader judge where it applies (transferability), could the trail be followed (dependability), and does it rest on the data rather than the researcher (confirmability).

MT-quality_criteria-how1.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-how1.text: 'Four questions are commonly put to qualitative work of this kind, credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability (Lincoln and Guba, 1985), and each is answered here with what was done' (3.7).

MT-quality_criteria-how2.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-how2.text: Credibility: three codings, the last two from the transcripts alone without the first coding's notes; each half read twice in the third coding, the second blind, agreeing on 112 of 130; every quotation verified against its transcript; disconfirming evidence required of both codings (3.7).

MT-quality_criteria-how3.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-how3.text: Transferability: eleven countries and the kinds of party the question needed, each described 'thickly enough, in Geertz's sense (1973), by code and by type, for a reader to judge where the findings travel' (3.7).

MT-quality_criteria-how4.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-how4.text: Dependability: every screening decision and card logged in Appendices E and H; every coded stance in Appendix I; the codes of the 117 and their settlements in Appendix L; the locker networks and test runs in Appendix M; every claim of the fifth link traced in a register Appendix O describes (3.7).

MT-quality_criteria-how5.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-how5.text: The register: 'Every claim the fifth link makes was entered in a register with its evidence, the source and page or the data file and row, and the step of the argument it supports' (3.5).

MT-quality_criteria-how6.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-how6.text: Confirmability: 'the coding's cautions (3.4) are carried into the text as written' (3.7).

MT-quality_criteria-how7.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-how7.text: The word 'validity' appears once, in Maxwell's interactive model (3.8); the thesis frames quality in Lincoln and Guba's terms.

MT-quality_criteria-why.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-why.text: They are the questions 'commonly put to qualitative work of this kind' (3.7).

MT-quality_criteria-not.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-not.text: Positivist validity and reliability are not used as the frame (3.7). Member checking (returning findings to participants) is not mentioned.

MT-quality_criteria-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-quality_criteria-analogy.text: A food hygiene inspection with four headings: is it safe, could it be served elsewhere, are the records kept, and is the kitchen judged on its own state rather than the chef's word.

MV-quality_criteria-v3.speaker: dr_tally
MV-quality_criteria-v3.text: Did you take your findings back to participants?

MQ-quality_criteria-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-quality_criteria-q1.text: Which is NOT one of Lincoln and Guba's four criteria as 3.7 applies them?

MG-quality_criteria.speaker: sam
MG-quality_criteria.text: Member checking is not mentioned, and the full register and systematised-review log are held by the author rather than appended.

MT-raw_agreement-term.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-term.text: Intercoder agreement as raw agreement (112 of 130)

MT-raw_agreement-plain.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-plain.text: Raw agreement is the simple share of decisions on which two codings match. Unlike some measures, it does not adjust for matches that would happen by chance.

MT-raw_agreement-how1.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-how1.text: 'Over the twenty-six, 112 of 130 stances were read the same way twice, an agreement of eighty-six per cent' (3.4). 130 = 26 transcripts x 5 concepts.

MT-raw_agreement-how2.speaker: sam
