MT-raw_agreement-how2.text: By concept (Table 3.6): overlap 20 of 26; boundary 20; what binds 25; power 22; time 25.

MT-raw_agreement-how3.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-how3.text: By half: A1 to A13, 53 of 65; B1 to B13, 59 of 65 (Table 3.6).

MT-raw_agreement-how4.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-how4.text: The largest share of the A half's differences, five of twelve, falls on the boundary concept, 'where freight or operating data pooled under a binder can be read as crossing the line or as held at it'; every such difference runs the same way, so 'the two readings agree on the facts and differ on one rule' (3.4; Table 3.6 note).

MT-raw_agreement-how5.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-how5.text: A transcript counts as agreement when both readings give the same stance; qualifiers such as 'weak' or 'qualified' do not count as disagreement (Table 3.6).

MT-raw_agreement-why.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-why.text: 'The figure is reported as raw agreement and not as a chance-corrected coefficient, because with four possible stances, thirteen transcripts to a half and a fifth concept, time, on which most transcripts are silent, a coefficient would say less than the list of the eighteen differences themselves, which Table 3.6 gives by concept and by half and the paragraph beneath it by transcript' (3.4).

MT-raw_agreement-not.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-not.text: A chance-corrected coefficient such as Krippendorff's alpha, used instead for the 117 arrangements (3.4).

MT-raw_agreement-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-raw_agreement-analogy.text: Two referees reviewing the same match footage: you could compute a statistic, but with few calls it is clearer to list the eighteen they disagreed on.

MV-raw_agreement-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-raw_agreement-v1.text: Eighty-six per cent raw agreement doesn't correct for chance. Why should I trust it?

MV-raw_agreement-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-raw_agreement-v2.text: Where do the readings disagree most?

MQ-raw_agreement-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-raw_agreement-q1.text: Why is the transcript agreement reported as raw agreement?

MQ-raw_agreement-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-raw_agreement-q2.text: On which concepts did the two readings agree on 25 of 26 transcripts?

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-term.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-term.text: Reading cards, the second reading, and counts of silence

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-plain.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-plain.text: A reading card is a structured note made for each paper, recording what it says on each point the review cares about. 'Silent' means the reading found nothing on that point, not that the paper denies it.

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how1.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how1.text: A card was made for every included paper; the 241 were carded 170 from full text, 63 from abstracts and 8 from bibliographic records, with quotations located to the page wherever the full text was carded (3.2; Table 3.3).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how2.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how2.text: The cards were read a second time in September 2026, when full texts obtained that month were read and those cards set again; the counts of 2.2 are from the second reading, with the first reading's counts of silence beside them (3.2).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how3.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how3.text: Silence fell on the second reading: on the boundary of sharing from 36 to 26, on overlap from 128 to 108, on time from 138 to 133 (2.2).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how4.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how4.text: A card marked 'not in text' was counted as silent (2.2).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how5.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how5.text: 'A card counts as silent if its reading found nothing on the point. A reading can miss things, so the real counts of silence in 2.2 may be lower than those given there' (3.7; the same caution in 2.2 and 7.4).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how6.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-how6.text: On every link, papers supporting the chain outnumber those against by more than three to one (2.2).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-why.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-why.text: 'Not in text' counts as silent 'because a paper written for another purpose may simply not cover that concept, and this must not be read as a finding against it' (2.2). The second reading took in full texts obtained in September 2026 (3.2).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-not.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-not.text: Counting 'not in text' as evidence against (rejected, 2.2).

MT-reading_cards_and_silence-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-reading_cards_and_silence-analogy.text: A library catalogue card per book: a blank line means the cataloguer found nothing, not that the book has nothing.

MV-reading_cards_and_silence-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-reading_cards_and_silence-v1.text: Sixty-three of your cards come from abstracts. Doesn't that understate what the papers say?

MV-reading_cards_and_silence-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-reading_cards_and_silence-v2.text: Why count 'not in text' as silent rather than as against?

MQ-reading_cards_and_silence-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-reading_cards_and_silence-q1.text: After the second reading, how many of the 241 cards were silent on overlap?

MT-reflexivity-plain.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-plain.text: The researcher's continual examination of how they themselves shaped what they found, and what they did about it.

MT-reflexivity-how1.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how1.text: Reflexivity 'in Finlay's sense (2002) of the researcher's continual examination of how they shaped what they found, has six objects here' (3.7).

MT-reflexivity-how2.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how2.text: 1: the 2023 review, whose string reproduced the field's blind spot until the corrected strings exposed it.

MT-reflexivity-how3.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how3.text: 2: the framework of 2024, built on the four pillars, which the data overturned; 'the guide asked about trust because the field did'.

MT-reflexivity-how4.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how4.text: 3: the theme the interviewer seeded: brand, raised in five interviews, declined in all five, counted as declined.

MT-reflexivity-how5.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how5.text: 4: the positions relayed between interviews, so agreement across transcripts is partly the interviewer's doing; the second coding marked where it happened.

MT-reflexivity-how6.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how6.text: 5: the author's first picture of the fifth link, hours allocated by a city to named companies, taken apart by his own questioning (Ostrom, 1990, p. 204; Stad Gent, 2016, p. 112).

MT-reflexivity-how7.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how7.text: 6: GREEN-LOG: in 2023 the author spent six months on spatio-temporal demand prediction for another of its living labs (work package 2, task 2.2); the thesis draws on none of that work and cites the Athens living lab from its published evaluation (3.7; 1.6).

MT-reflexivity-how8.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how8.text: What was done about each 'is the method itself': string corrected and both trails kept; pillars made findings; seeded theme counted against; relayed positions marked; first picture tested and replaced (3.7).

MT-reflexivity-how9.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-how9.text: 'The exposure no procedure removes is that the author interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim the later codings tested' (3.7).

MT-reflexivity-why.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-why.text: Finlay (2002); and in 1.6, the order of emergence is set out 'because a framework that came out of the data is a stronger claim to conceptualisation than one fixed before the data arrived, as long as the thesis shows how it came about'.

MT-reflexivity-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-reflexivity-analogy.text: A referee reviewing footage of his own decisions, noting where his position on the pitch may have hidden a foul.

MV-reflexivity-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-reflexivity-v1.text: What are the objects of your reflexivity?

MV-reflexivity-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-reflexivity-v1-ans.text: Six: the 2023 review's string, which reproduced the field's blind spot; the four-pillar framework the data overturned; brand, which I seeded and which was declined in all five interviews; the positions I relayed between interviews; my own first picture of the fifth link, hours for named companies, which my questioning took apart; and my six months on GREEN-LOG, which the thesis draws on nowhere (3.7).

MV-reflexivity-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-reflexivity-v2.text: What exposure can't your procedures remove?

MV-reflexivity-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-reflexivity-v2-ans.text: That I interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim the later codings tested. My answer is the two later codings made without the first coding's notes, the blind second reading of every transcript, and the requirement of evidence against; 3.4 says how far that reaches (3.7).

MQ-reflexivity-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-reflexivity-q1.text: In whose sense does 3.7 use reflexivity?

MQ-reflexivity-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-reflexivity-q2.text: Which of these is one of the six objects of reflexivity?

MT-research_paradigm-term.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-term.text: Research paradigm (ontology, epistemology, mode of inference)

MT-research_paradigm-plain.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-plain.text: A paradigm is a set of starting assumptions: what exists (ontology), how it can be known (epistemology), and so how to reason from evidence (mode of inference). It decides what will count as a finding.

MT-research_paradigm-how1.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-how1.text: Table 3.2 compares three paradigms 'in the terms Guba and Lincoln (1994) use to compare paradigms, adapted' (3.1).

MT-research_paradigm-how2.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-how2.text: Guba and Lincoln's four positions are reduced to two, positivism and constructivism, 'the latter labelled interpretivist here as it commonly is'; the third column is drawn from the critical realist literature (Fleetwood, 2005; Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992; Easton, 2010) (3.1).

MT-research_paradigm-how3.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-how3.text: The rows compared are ontology, epistemology, mode of inference, what counts as a finding, how findings generalise, the researcher's position, and where this thesis sits (Table 3.2).

MT-research_paradigm-how4.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-how4.text: Adopted: critical realist. Rejected: positivist and interpretivist, each with its reason in the last row (Table 3.2).

MT-research_paradigm-why.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-why.text: 'Critical realism was chosen for three reasons, and each rival position fails one of them' (3.1); the three reasons are set out under critical realism. The thesis says that Guba and Lincoln's four positions 'are reduced to two, positivism and constructivism' (3.1), but not why.

MT-research_paradigm-not.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-not.text: Positivism and interpretivism, both rejected in Table 3.2. Guba and Lincoln's other two positions are not discussed.

MT-research_paradigm-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-research_paradigm-analogy.text: Choosing which instrument you will trust before you go out to measure: a tape measure, a conversation and an accident investigator's reconstruction each make different things count as evidence.

MV-research_paradigm-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-research_paradigm-v1.text: State your ontology and your epistemology, one sentence each.

MV-research_paradigm-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-research_paradigm-v2.text: Guba and Lincoln compare four paradigms. Why do you compare only three?

MQ-research_paradigm-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-research_paradigm-q1.text: In Table 3.2, which paradigm's mode of inference is 'induction: accounts built up from what participants say'?

MQ-research_paradigm-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-research_paradigm-q2.text: How does Table 3.2 adapt Guba and Lincoln (1994)?

MG-research_paradigm.speaker: sam
MG-research_paradigm.text: Why Guba and Lincoln's four positions are reduced to two is not stated.

MT-retroduction-plain.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-plain.text: Reasoning backwards from a recurring pattern to what must be true for that pattern to occur, then checking that explanation against the cases that should break it.

MT-retroduction-how1.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-how1.text: 'Explanation is retroductive: from a pattern that recurs across cases to the mechanism that would produce it' (3.1).

MT-retroduction-how2.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-how2.text: Start: the regularity in twenty-six accounts and one city's record (3.1).

MT-retroduction-how3.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-how3.text: Ask: not 'what caused it in one case' but 'what must be true for it to keep happening' (3.1; Danermark et al., 2002; Sayer, 1992).

MT-retroduction-how4.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-how4.text: Answer: a mechanism, overlap and binding (3.1).

MT-retroduction-how5.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-how5.text: Test: check the mechanism 'against the cases where it should have worked and did not'; 'the interviews were searched as carefully for evidence against the mechanism as for evidence for it'; the mechanism tested against Ghent, and the holder against the 117 arrangements, forty-three locker networks and the rules (3.1).

MT-retroduction-how6.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-how6.text: Output: a proposition, because 'a mechanism inferred from accounts is retroduced and not observed' (7.4).

MT-retroduction-why.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-why.text: 'Critical realism reasons by retroduction' (3.1), and 'the explanation sought is a mechanism that can be tested against the cases that should break it, which is retroduction, not induction' (3.1).

MT-retroduction-not.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-not.text: Deduction (positivist: hypotheses tested against measurement) and induction (interpretivist: accounts built up from what participants say) (Table 3.2). The thesis does not mention abduction.

MT-retroduction-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-retroduction-analogy.text: A mechanic hears the same knock in many cars, works back to what must be loose for that knock to occur, then checks cars where that part is tight to confirm the knock is absent.

MX-retroduction-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-retroduction-b1.text: Across twenty-six interviews, one pattern keeps returning: rivals who share customers refuse to pool.

MX-retroduction-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-retroduction-b2.text: Retroduction runs backwards: what must be true for this pattern to keep happening?

MX-retroduction-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-retroduction-b3.text: The answer is a mechanism: overlap, with nothing outside to outweigh the exposure.

MX-retroduction-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-retroduction-b4.text: Then the test: look for the cases that should break it.

MX-retroduction-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-retroduction-b5.text: Where something binds rivals from outside, they collaborate. The mechanism survives.

MX-retroduction-b6.speaker: marigold
MX-retroduction-b6.text: What comes out is a proposition about a mechanism, offered for others to test.

MV-retroduction-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-retroduction-v1.text: Explain retroduction to someone outside research.

MV-retroduction-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-retroduction-v1-ans.text: It's reasoning back from a pattern to what must be so for the pattern to recur. I saw refusals recur wherever rivals' customers overlapped, asked what must be true for that, and answered with overlap and binding. Then I set that answer against the cases that should break it, which is why the evidence against was coded as deliberately as the evidence for (3.1).

MV-retroduction-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-retroduction-v2.text: How is retroduction different from induction?

MV-retroduction-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-retroduction-v2-ans.text: Induction builds an account up from what participants say. Retroduction asks what must be so for an observed regularity to be possible, names a mechanism and tests it against the cases where it should have fired and did not: here Ghent, the 117 arrangements, forty-three locker networks and the rules (Table 3.2; 3.1).

MV-retroduction-v3.speaker: dr_tally
MV-retroduction-v3.text: Isn't what you describe really abduction?

MV-retroduction-v3-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-retroduction-v3-ans.text: I name my mode of inference as retroduction, the mode critical realism gives this kind of work, following Danermark and colleagues and Sayer, and the thesis does not discuss abduction. What I can state exactly is what I did: from the regularity to the mechanism that would produce it, then tested against the cases that should break it (3.1).

MQ-retroduction-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-retroduction-q1.text: What question does retroduction put to a regularity, as 3.1 states it?

MQ-retroduction-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-retroduction-q2.text: What does 7.4 say is the cost of a mechanism inferred from accounts?

MG-retroduction.speaker: sal
MG-retroduction.text: Abduction is not discussed. If an examiner raises it, say what you did rather than debate labels.

MT-robustness_and_replications-term.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-term.text: Robustness checks and the two replications

MT-robustness_and_replications-plain.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-plain.text: Repeating an analysis in ways that should not change the answer if it is sound: running it twice independently, removing one case at a time, recoding doubtful cases the hard way, and re-checking every calculation.

MT-robustness_and_replications-how1.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-how1.text: Two replications: 'Each pass of version 2 was paired with one of version 3, and the two pairs were run separately, as two replications, and not merged, so that a result must hold in both' (3.4).

MT-robustness_and_replications-how2.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-how2.text: Drop-one: 'Each result was checked by dropping each case in turn' (3.4).

MT-robustness_and_replications-how3.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-how3.text: Hard recoding: 'and by recoding every helper and every public body as never neutral' (3.4).

MT-robustness_and_replications-how4.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-how4.text: Recomputation: 'After the analysis every computation, the agreement figures, the comparison and its checks, was checked again against the settled codes; the faults found, among them a counting error, were corrected, and every figure in this thesis is from the corrected computations, which Appendix L reports' (3.4).

MT-robustness_and_replications-how5.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-how5.text: Appendix L reports that, dropping each case in turn, necessity ranges from 0.89 to 1.00 in each replication, lowest without H1-11.

MT-robustness_and_replications-why.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-why.text: Replications are kept apart 'so that a result must hold in both' (3.4). The thesis gives no separate reason for the drop-one and recoding checks.

MT-robustness_and_replications-not.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-not.text: Merging the passes into one data set (rejected, 3.4).

MT-robustness_and_replications-analogy.speaker: manny
MT-robustness_and_replications-analogy.text: Two engineers each building the bridge model separately, then taking out one strut at a time to see if it still stands.

MV-robustness_and_replications-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-robustness_and_replications-v1.text: What is a replication in your analysis?

MV-robustness_and_replications-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-robustness_and_replications-v2.text: You found a counting error. What happened?

MQ-robustness_and_replications-q1.speaker: manny
MQ-robustness_and_replications-q1.text: Why were the two replications not merged?

MQ-robustness_and_replications-q2.speaker: manny
MQ-robustness_and_replications-q2.text: Which of these was NOT one of the robustness checks in 3.4?

MG-robustness_and_replications.speaker: manny
MG-robustness_and_replications.text: The results of the drop-one and recoding checks are not given in the main text, only in Appendix L.

MT-rule_1a-term.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-term.text: Rule 1a (the trustee rule), and why it is reported both ways

MT-rule_1a-plain.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-plain.text: A coding rule added after the results were seen. Because a late rule can bend a result towards what the researcher expects, every result is reported with it and without it.

MT-rule_1a-how1.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-how1.text: The rule: 'Where a neutral trustee runs a scheme (it selects the members, holds each party's data and hires the operator), the trustee is coded as the holder, and the operator it hires as a helper working for it' (7.4).

MT-rule_1a-how2.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-how2.text: Why it arose: once version 3 stopped counting the trustee as a wall, 'the coding rule that gives the holder to whoever holds the goods made the hired operator the holder in the three rows that describe the one trustee-run shipper network (H.1 11, 17 and 37), and the trustee was coded nowhere' (3.7).

MT-rule_1a-how3.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-how3.text: 'The rule was added after the results were seen' (3.7; 4.4; 7.4). Appendix L dates it to 28 October 2026.

MT-rule_1a-how4.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-how4.text: 'Rule 1a applies to every row, and every result is reported both with it and without it (4.4, Appendix L)' (3.7).

MT-rule_1a-how5.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-how5.text: With it: 9 of 10 running rows meet the necessity bar; neutral holders run in 5 of 6 rows. Without it the three trustee rows drop out, 'because the transcripts do not show whether the operator each trustee hired sells to the parties' customers': 6 of 7, below the bar; neutral holders 2 of 3 (4.4; Table 7.1).

MT-rule_1a-how6.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-how6.text: 'The interviews support the holder only under that rule' (4.4).

MT-rule_1a-how7.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-how7.text: Further research: the rule 'should be applied as it stands to arrangements this thesis did not code, so that the interviews' support for the holder is tested on rows the rule was not written from' (7.5).

MT-rule_1a-why.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-why.text: Both results are given because of the late addition: 'That late addition is why both results are given, here and in Appendix L' (4.4); and the codebook rule that 'where a change alters a result both results are reported' (3.4). The rule itself was needed because, without it, the trustee 'was coded nowhere' (3.7).

MT-rule_1a-not.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-not.text: Reporting only the result with the rule (rejected), or dropping the rule (also reported).

MT-rule_1a-analogy.speaker: manny
MT-rule_1a-analogy.text: A referee who changes an offside rule at half-time must publish the score under both rules, and the new rule must then be tried in matches it wasn't written for.

MX-rule_1a-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-rule_1a-b1.text: Three accounts describe one shipper network run by a neutral trustee.

MX-rule_1a-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-rule_1a-b2.text: Version 3 moved the trustee out of 'wall' and into 'holder'.

MX-rule_1a-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-rule_1a-b3.text: But an older rule gave the holder to whoever holds the goods: the hired van.

MX-rule_1a-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-rule_1a-b4.text: The trustee was coded nowhere. Rule 1a, added after the results, codes it as holder.

MX-rule_1a-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-rule_1a-b5.text: With rule 1a: nine of ten running rows meet the bar. Without it: six of seven.

MX-rule_1a-b6.speaker: marigold
MX-rule_1a-b6.text: Because the rule came late, every result is reported both ways.

MV-rule_1a-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-rule_1a-v1.text: Your holder result depends on a rule you added after seeing the results. Isn't that circular?

MV-rule_1a-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-rule_1a-v1-ans.text: It would be if I hid it. The rule was added after the results were seen, I say so in 3.7, 4.4 and 7.4, it applies to every row, and every result is reported with and without it. With it, nine of ten; without it, six of seven, below the bar. So I claim only that the interviews support the holder under that rule, and the next study should apply the rule as it stands to arrangements it wasn't written from (4.4; 7.5).

MV-rule_1a-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-rule_1a-v2.text: Why was the rule needed at all?

MV-rule_1a-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-rule_1a-v2-ans.text: Because once version 3 stopped counting the trustee as a wall, the rule that gives the holder to whoever holds the goods sent the holder code to the operator the trustee hired, in the three rows on the one trustee-run shipper network, and the trustee was coded nowhere. Rule 1a codes the trustee as the holder and the operator as its helper (3.7).

MV-rule_1a-v3.speaker: dr_tally
MV-rule_1a-v3.text: Why do the three rows drop out entirely without the rule?

MV-rule_1a-v3-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-rule_1a-v3-ans.text: Because the transcripts don't show whether the operator each trustee hired sells to the parties' customers, so without the rule the holder can't be classed as neutral or not (4.4).

MQ-rule_1a-q2.speaker: manny
MQ-rule_1a-q2.text: How many rows of Appendix H does rule 1a change?

MT-saturation-term.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-term.text: Saturation (data saturation, reached by kind of party)

MT-saturation-plain.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-plain.text: The point at which new interviews stop adding anything new. Different authors mean different things by it, so a study should say which kind it reached.

MT-saturation-how1.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-how1.text: Saunders and colleagues (2018) 'distinguish four things saturation can mean, theoretical, inductive thematic, a priori thematic and data saturation' (3.3).

MT-saturation-how2.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-how2.text: 'What was reached here is the fourth in their terms, ‘identifying redundancy in the data’, the point at which a new participant of a kind described arrangements and refusals the set already held' (3.3).

MT-saturation-how3.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-how3.text: 'It was reached by kind of party and not by count, which is why the carriers, at four voices, are the one kind 3.7 calls thin' (3.3).

MT-saturation-how4.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-how4.text: Guest, Bunce and Johnson's (2006) finding that most themes appear within the first dozen interviews 'is not relied on, because it was reached on a homogeneous sample, and this one was chosen to be the opposite' (3.3).

MT-saturation-why.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-why.text: As above: saturation is defined so the claim can be checked, and judged by kind of party because the sample was deliberately varied (3.3).

MT-saturation-not.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-not.text: Guest, Bunce and Johnson's dozen-interview rule (3.3).

MT-saturation-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-saturation-analogy.text: Tasting a soup from every pot in a kitchen: you stop when each pot's next spoonful tastes like the last, not after a fixed number of spoonfuls overall.

MV-saturation-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-saturation-v1-ans.text: Data saturation in Saunders and colleagues' sense, identifying redundancy in the data: the point at which a new participant of a kind described arrangements and refusals the set already held. It was reached by kind of party, not by count, which is why the carriers, at four voices, are the one kind I call thin (3.3; 3.7).

MV-saturation-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-saturation-v2.text: Most themes appear within twelve interviews, according to Guest and colleagues. Why not cite that?

MV-saturation-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-saturation-v2-ans.text: Because their finding was reached on a homogeneous sample, and mine was chosen to be the opposite, so I don't rely on it (3.3).

MQ-saturation-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-saturation-q1.text: Which of Saunders and colleagues' four kinds of saturation does the thesis claim?

MQ-saturation-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-saturation-q2.text: Why is Guest, Bunce and Johnson's dozen-interview finding not relied on?

MT-scenario_model-term.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-term.text: The scenario model (a scenario, not a forecast)

MT-scenario_model-plain.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-plain.text: A worked example that sets out what a policy might cost and save under stated assumptions, with low, central and high values, rather than a prediction of what will happen.

MT-scenario_model-how1.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-how1.text: For 'one notional council area of 50,000 households, as a scenario and not a forecast' (3.5).

MT-scenario_model-how2.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-how2.text: 'Each input has a low, a central and a high value, a worst case is added, every input is sourced or marked as an assumption, and only the increment over the redirection to nearby points that already happens is counted' (3.5).

MT-scenario_model-how3.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-how3.text: Time valued at the Department for Transport's value for non-work time, £7.08 an hour; car emissions at 0.167 kg of carbon dioxide equivalent a kilometre (3.5).

MT-scenario_model-how4.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-how4.text: Central case: about 33,600 depot trips and 28,000 hours of residents' time saved a year (about 9,100 hours by households without a car), worth about £198,000; carriers save about £106,000 on redeliveries; checking 60 points at £700 costs £42,000; net about £262,000 (6.3).

MT-scenario_model-how5.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-how5.text: Low case: adds nothing, leaving the cost of checking 30 points at £400, £12,000. Worst case: low benefits with 100 points at £1,500, the council £150,000 a year down (6.3).

MT-scenario_model-how6.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-how6.text: 'Eight of the thirteen inputs are assumptions, and the result turns on the share of missed parcels redirected and the time each trip saves' (6.3).

MT-scenario_model-how7.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-how7.text: A check costs about £400 to £1,500 a point a year (6.3). Inputs, sources and formulas are in Appendix N (3.5).

MT-scenario_model-why.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-why.text: The thesis presents it as setting out 'what the rule proposed in 6.3 ... would cost and save' (3.5). It does not argue for the scenario method against alternatives. 3.7 calls it 'a worked example on an assumed share of what is redirected today'.

MT-scenario_model-analogy.speaker: penny
MT-scenario_model-analogy.text: A household budget drawn up for a lean month, a normal month and a bad month: it shows what depends on what, not what next month will be.

MX-scenario_model-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-scenario_model-b1.text: What would the rule cost and save? A scenario, not a forecast.

MX-scenario_model-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-scenario_model-b2.text: Only the extra is counted: parcels some residents already collect nearby are left out.

MX-scenario_model-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-scenario_model-b3.text: Central case: fewer depot trips, hours saved, carriers' redeliveries cut, minus the checking cost.

MX-scenario_model-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-scenario_model-b4.text: Net, about two hundred and sixty thousand pounds a year.

MX-scenario_model-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-scenario_model-b5.text: Low case: nothing gained, only the checking cost. Worst case: well below zero.

MX-scenario_model-b6.speaker: marigold
MX-scenario_model-b6.text: Eight of thirteen inputs are assumptions. Two decide the answer.

MV-scenario_model-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-scenario_model-v1.text: Eight of your thirteen inputs are assumptions. What is the scenario worth?

MV-scenario_model-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-scenario_model-v1-ans.text: It is a worked example, not a forecast, and I say which inputs are assumptions and that the result turns on two of them, the share of missed parcels redirected and the time each trip saves. It shows the range: about £262,000 a year net in the central case, nothing but a £12,000 checking cost in the low case, and £150,000 down in the worst case (6.3; 3.7).

MV-scenario_model-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-scenario_model-v2-ans.text: Because some missed parcels are already redirected to nearby points, so only what the rule adds beyond that redirection is counted (3.5).

MQ-scenario_model-q1.speaker: penny
MQ-scenario_model-q1.text: In the central case, what is the net value a year?

MQ-scenario_model-q2.speaker: penny
MQ-scenario_model-q2.text: What value of time does the scenario use?

MQ-scenario_model-q3.speaker: penny
MQ-scenario_model-q3.text: How many of the thirteen inputs are assumptions?

MG-scenario_model.speaker: penny
MG-scenario_model.text: The scenario method itself is not justified against alternatives; it is presented as a worked example.

MT-scott_four_tests-term.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-term.text: Scott's four tests for documents: authenticity, credibility, representativeness, meaning

MT-scott_four_tests-plain.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-plain.text: Four questions to ask of any document used as evidence: is it genuine, is it believable for the use made of it, is it typical of what it stands for, and is its meaning understood correctly.

MT-scott_four_tests-how1.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-how1.text: 'Read as documents, they pass the four tests Scott (1990) sets, and the passing is stated because it bounds the use made of them' (3.5).

MT-scott_four_tests-how2.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-how2.text: Authentic: 'the city's own plans, published under its name, held as the PDFs from which Appendix J reproduces the extracts used'.

MT-scott_four_tests-how3.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-how3.text: Credible 'for the use made of them, which is as the regime's statement of what it allocates and what it expected, not as evidence of what happened on the street'.

MT-scott_four_tests-how4.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-how4.text: Representative 'of the regime's written record and not of the regime, since the permit register and the enforcement records were not read, which 3.7 carries as a limit'.

MT-scott_four_tests-how5.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-how5.text: Meaning: held to the Dutch by translating only the extracts used and setting the Dutch beside the English in Appendix J (Temple and Young, 2004).

MT-scott_four_tests-how6.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-how6.text: The rules read for the holder 'pass Scott's tests as the Ghent plans do, as the issuing bodies' own texts and as statements of the rule rather than of its working' (3.5).

MT-scott_four_tests-why.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-why.text: 'The passing is stated because it bounds the use made of them' (3.5).

MT-scott_four_tests-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-scott_four_tests-analogy.text: Checking a will: is it genuine, is it the testator's considered wish, is it the latest version, and do we read its old-fashioned wording correctly.

MV-scott_four_tests-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-scott_four_tests-v1.text: How did you judge the Ghent documents as evidence?

MV-scott_four_tests-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-scott_four_tests-v2.text: The plans represent the city's written record, not the regime itself. What does that cost you?

MQ-scott_four_tests-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-scott_four_tests-q1.text: For what use are the Ghent plans called credible?

MQ-scott_four_tests-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-scott_four_tests-q2.text: Why are the plans representative of the record but not of the regime?

MT-search_string-term.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-term.text: The search string and the review's blind spot

MT-search_string-plain.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-plain.text: A search string is the exact combination of words and logic (AND, OR) fed to a database. It decides what the review can see; work phrased outside it is invisible.

MT-search_string-how1.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-how1.text: The 2022 string: ("collaborative" OR "multimodal") AND ("last mile") AND ("urban" OR "city") AND ("logistics" OR "delivery") (2.1).

MT-search_string-how2.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-how2.text: Its forty-nine described 'a set of strategies for a small group of parcel carriers. That was not what the string had asked for. It was what the string could see' (2.1).

MT-search_string-how3.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-how3.text: Its reach was tested before any new search: twelve papers sit inside the field's own citation trail on horizontal collaboration (Appendix F); run again in OpenAlex, the 2022 string returns none of them; the 2023 review held one, added by hand (2.2).

MT-search_string-how4.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-how4.text: Three of the twelve come from outside freight, so 'the case that the 2022 string missed the collaboration literature rests on the other nine' (2.2).

MT-search_string-how5.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-how5.text: Five corrected strings were added in September 2026: horizontal collaboration and cooperation, the noun collaboration, carrier and shipper terms, consolidation and micro-hub terms, and time-window terms (Table 3.3).

MT-search_string-how6.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-how6.text: Of the 231 update papers not among the forty-nine, the 2022 string returns only 39, and 192 fall outside its terms; 33 of the 39 are dated before 2018 or from 2023; four of the remaining six, and two others, reached the 238 that passed the 2023 journal stage. So, 'with at most eight exceptions', the 2023 review did not weigh these papers and reject them (2.2).

MT-search_string-how7.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-how7.text: Both strings are reported side by side and both trails kept (2.2; Appendix E). The 2023 string is the first object of reflexivity (3.7).

MT-search_string-why.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-why.text: The corrected strings 'name the subject the original could not see' (3.2), 'in the collaboration literature's own terms' (2.2). Both are kept because 'the two searches map two bodies of work that barely meet, the last-mile literature and the collaboration literature, and the thesis needs both' (2.2).

MT-search_string-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-search_string-analogy.text: A fishing net cut for one species: it lands plenty, but a whole shoal of another kind swims through, and the catch looks complete.

MX-search_string-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-search_string-b1.text: A search string is a net. Its words decide which papers it can catch.

MX-search_string-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-search_string-b2.text: The 2022 net required 'last mile'. It caught papers on carriers' delivery strategies.

MX-search_string-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-search_string-b3.text: Papers that never said 'last mile' were invisible to it, however central to collaboration.

MX-search_string-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-search_string-b4.text: The test: twelve papers from the field's own citation trail. The old net caught none.

MX-search_string-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-search_string-b5.text: Corrected strings named the subject in its own words, and 241 papers came in.

MV-search_string-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-search_string-v1.text: How did you show the 2022 string missed the literature, rather than just assert it?

MV-search_string-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-search_string-v1-ans.text: I tested its reach before running a new search. Twelve papers sit in the field's own citation trail on horizontal collaboration, and run again in OpenAlex the 2022 string returns none of them. Then, of the 231 update papers not in the forty-nine, it returns only 39; 192 fall outside its terms. With at most eight exceptions, the 2023 review didn't weigh those papers and reject them; it couldn't find them (2.2).

MV-search_string-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-search_string-v2.text: Three of your twelve test papers aren't about freight. Doesn't that inflate the case?

MV-search_string-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-search_string-v2-ans.text: They are not about freight, so a last-mile string could not be expected to find them, and I say the case rests on the other nine. The three are read because each tests, outside freight, a condition the freight papers raise (2.2).

MQ-search_string-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-search_string-q1.text: Of the 231 update papers not among the forty-nine, how many does the 2022 string return?

MQ-search_string-q2.speaker: ada
MQ-search_string-q2.text: Which of these did the corrected strings add?

MT-semi_structured_interview-term.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-term.text: Semi-structured interview (the guide and the working script)

MT-semi_structured_interview-plain.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-plain.text: An interview with a fixed set of themes but a free order and free follow-up questions, so the conversation can follow what the participant knows.

MT-semi_structured_interview-how1.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-how1.text: The instrument approved by the School's ethics committee on 22 February 2024 asked fourteen questions under seven headings, two to a heading (3.3; Appendix A).

MT-semi_structured_interview-how2.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-how2.text: Three headings framed the conversation ('Background and Experience with HC', 'Challenges and Solutions', 'Future Perspectives'); the four between them were the pillars of the registration: 'Trust and Partnership', 'Operational Efficiency', 'Innovation in Collaboration', 'Sustainability Outcomes' (3.3).

MT-semi_structured_interview-how3.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-how3.text: A working script of twenty-three prompts in ten stages, from introduction and consent through role, collaborations known, drivers, blocks, outcomes and whom else to ask, sat beside the guide in every interview (3.3).

MT-semi_structured_interview-how4.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-how4.text: The guide was built in the sequence Kallio and colleagues (2016) describe, from prerequisites and prior knowledge to a preliminary guide and its complete form (the fourteen-question guide and the twenty-three-prompt script) (3.3).

MT-semi_structured_interview-how5.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-how5.text: The interviews were conducted as Brinkmann and Kvale (2015) describe the form: 'a guide that fixes the themes and leaves the order and the follow-up to the conversation' (3.3).

MT-semi_structured_interview-how6.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-how6.text: The guide had allowed forty-five to sixty minutes; the median was forty-three, and fourteen closed sooner, 'most because the participant had said what they had come to say, though a call is easier to end than a visit' (3.3).

MT-semi_structured_interview-why.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-why.text: The script 'let the conversation follow the participant rather than the headings' (3.3). 'The guide asked about trust because the field did; what the participants answered is in Chapter 4, and it is why the pillars are findings in this thesis rather than its frame' (3.3). The thesis does not set the semi-structured form against structured or unstructured interviews.

MT-semi_structured_interview-not.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-not.text: No alternative interview form is named. In hindsight (7.4): 'a guide written after the fact would have asked about overlap and time directly and found less than it was told, because the participants brought both unprompted'.

MT-semi_structured_interview-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-semi_structured_interview-analogy.text: A walking tour with a list of landmarks but no fixed route: every landmark gets visited, in whatever order the guide's companion leads.

MV-semi_structured_interview-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-semi_structured_interview-v1.text: Your guide was built on four pillars you later abandoned. Doesn't that taint the data?

MV-semi_structured_interview-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-semi_structured_interview-v2.text: Fourteen interviews ended before the forty-five minutes you planned. Is that a problem?

MQ-semi_structured_interview-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-semi_structured_interview-q1.text: How many questions, under how many headings, did the approved guide ask?

MQ-semi_structured_interview-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-semi_structured_interview-q2.text: Whose description of the semi-structured form does 3.3 follow?

MG-semi_structured_interview.speaker: sam
MG-semi_structured_interview.text: Why semi-structured rather than structured or unstructured is not argued.

MT-sign_test-term.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-term.text: Sign test: holding the carrier fixed

MT-sign_test-plain.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-plain.text: A simple test of direction: for each case, record only whether it leans one way or the other, ignore ties, and ask whether one direction wins more often than a coin toss would give.

MT-sign_test-how1.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-how1.text: 'The same carrier, by group and by national name, compared across networks of both kinds by a sign test, which holds the carrier fixed though not a network's price, terms or siting' (3.5).

MT-sign_test-how2.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-how2.text: By carrier group: of the 19 groups facing both kinds, 7 deliver into a larger share of the neutral-held networks, 2 into a larger share of the rival-held, 10 equal; p = .18 (5.2).

MT-sign_test-how3.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-how3.text: By national name: 10 against 2, 9 equal; p = .039 (5.2).

MT-sign_test-how4.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-how4.text: A national name is each name under which a carrier delivers, so the arms of one group, such as DHL's, count apart; 'because those arms share an owner they are not independent of one another, and the count by group is the stricter of the two' (5.2).

MT-sign_test-how5.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-how5.text: 'The same-carrier check gives the direction and does not prove it' (5.2).

MT-sign_test-how6.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-how6.text: Holding the network constant as well 'needs locker price, size and service data that the public sources used here do not hold' (7.4).

MT-sign_test-why.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-why.text: It holds the carrier fixed (3.5), removing differences between carriers from the comparison.

MT-sign_test-not.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-not.text: A quality-matched comparison holding the network fixed too, left to 7.5 (7.4).

MT-sign_test-analogy.speaker: lockie
MT-sign_test-analogy.text: Asking the same shoppers which of two shops they use more, so differences between shoppers drop out.

MV-sign_test-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-sign_test-v1.text: Why test the same carriers separately?

MV-sign_test-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-sign_test-v2.text: Why is the group count the stricter one?

MQ-sign_test-q1.speaker: lockie
MQ-sign_test-q1.text: By carrier group, how did the 19 groups facing both kinds split?

MQ-sign_test-q2.speaker: lockie
MQ-sign_test-q2.text: What does the sign test NOT hold fixed?

MT-size_vs_overlap-term.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-term.text: Separating size from overlap: mirror pairs and the count by size

MT-size_vs_overlap-plain.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-plain.text: To show that overlap, not size, sorts willingness, you need cases where size is held steady and overlap changes, and a count showing willing and unwilling firms at every size.

MT-size_vs_overlap-how1.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-how1.text: Sub-objectives 1A and 1B ask how willingness varies with operator size and with market overlap; 'the fieldwork was built to separate' them (4.2; 1.3).

MT-size_vs_overlap-how2.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-how2.text: Mirror pairs: 'the cases in which the same firm, or the same kind of firm, said yes and no in the same breath, one answer for each side of the line'; ten are set out in Table 4.2 (4.2).

MT-size_vs_overlap-how3.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-how3.text: Example: the same small cargo-bike firm refused a rival in its own city and was piloting with one in another town: 'It's not their city. There's no market competition' (B9) (4.2).

MT-size_vs_overlap-how4.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-how4.text: The count by size across both halves (Table 4.3): 'Read down either half, willing and unwilling firms appear at every size; read beside the overlap column of Appendix H, the willing cases are those in which the parties do not compete for the same customers or, where they do, something outside them stands between them' (4.2).

MT-size_vs_overlap-how5.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-how5.text: Overlap as the condition of refusal: 15 for, 1 against, 5 mixed, 5 silent (third coding); 12/0/7/7 (second reading) (Table 4.9).

MT-size_vs_overlap-how6.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-how6.text: The survey cannot separate size from overlap, because it asked nothing about overlap (5.3; 3.6).

MT-size_vs_overlap-why.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-why.text: The hypothesis carried into 2024 was size (the big fierce animal), and the twenty-six 'did not sustain it' (4.2). The codebook's falsifier for overlap is that 'size or brand explains willingness regardless of overlap' (Table 3.5).

MT-size_vs_overlap-not.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-not.text: Size as the variable that sorts willingness (the author's 2022 idea, corrected) (1.6; 4.2).

MT-size_vs_overlap-analogy.speaker: manny
MT-size_vs_overlap-analogy.text: To show it is the weather, not the driver, that causes skids, find the same driver skidding on ice and not on a dry road.

MV-size_vs_overlap-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-size_vs_overlap-v1.text: How did you separate size from overlap with only twenty-six interviews?

MV-size_vs_overlap-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-size_vs_overlap-v2.text: Your survey shows larger firms collaborate more. Doesn't that favour size?

MQ-size_vs_overlap-q1.speaker: manny
MQ-size_vs_overlap-q1.text: How many mirror pairs does Table 4.2 set out?

MQ-size_vs_overlap-q2.speaker: manny
MQ-size_vs_overlap-q2.text: Why can't the survey separate size from overlap?

MT-staged_design-plain.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-plain.text: Running research in steps, so that what each step finds shapes the next one.

MT-staged_design-how1.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-how1.text: Stage 1, 2022 and 2023: the systematic review, deductive under the four pillars; what its string could not see became the gap of 1.1 (3.1).

MT-staged_design-how2.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-how2.text: Stage 2, 2024 into 2025: twenty-six interviews in eleven countries, held July to September 2024, built on the four pillars, read inductively and coded three times between 2024 and 2026, with the survey running beside them from 22 February 2024 to 30 April 2025; the pillars became findings and the five links emerged across the three codings (3.1).

MT-staged_design-how3.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-how3.text: Figure 3.1, Stage 2: 'Each collaboration described became a row: 117 arrangements (Appendix H)'. So the 117 arrangements come from the interviews: 'each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration that a participant described is one row of Appendix H' (3.1).

MT-staged_design-how4.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-how4.text: Stage 4, October 2026: the fifth link in its final form, the holder: the 117 arrangements recoded, the rules and forty-three locker networks in sixteen countries reviewed, the networks compared, and a scenario built (3.1).

MT-staged_design-how5.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-how5.text: Figure 3.1 draws the stages 'in the multiphase form the design literature uses for sequential fieldwork (Creswell and Plano Clark, 2018)' (3.1).

MT-staged_design-how6.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-how6.text: Overall: 'qualitative at its core, with descriptive counts and statistical tests in its later stages' (Table 3.1).

MT-staged_design-why.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-why.text: 'Each stage's evidence feeding the next' (3.1). Maxwell's (2013) point, 'that the parts of a design act on one another rather than in sequence, is met in 3.8, where what changed between the stages is set out with its reason' (3.1). The thesis does not say why it describes the design as staged rather than as mixed methods.

MT-staged_design-not.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-not.text: The thesis does not call itself mixed methods; the phrase appears only in the title of Creswell and Plano Clark's book in the reference list.

MT-staged_design-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-staged_design-analogy.text: A relay where each runner's split sets the next runner's route: the review handed a gap to the interviews, the interviews handed a candidate rule to the documents, and so on.

MX-staged_design-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-staged_design-b1.text: The research ran in four stages, each handing its evidence to the next.

MX-staged_design-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-staged_design-b2.text: Stage one, 2022 to 2023: a review whose blind spot became the gap.

MX-staged_design-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-staged_design-b3.text: Stage two, 2024 to 2025: twenty-six interviews in eleven countries, a survey alongside.

MX-staged_design-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-staged_design-b4.text: Stage three: one city's permit hours, and the review run again with better strings.

MX-staged_design-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-staged_design-b5.text: Stage four, October 2026: who holds the shared point, tested on lockers and 117 arrangements.

MX-staged_design-b6.speaker: marigold
MX-staged_design-b6.text: Changes between stages were recorded, not hidden.

MV-staged_design-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-staged_design-v1-ans.text: I describe it as a staged design under a critical realist paradigm, qualitative at its core, with descriptive counts and statistical tests in its later stages, drawn in the multiphase form Creswell and Plano Clark use for sequential fieldwork. The survey is descriptive and gives scale; no link of the chain rests on it (Table 3.1; 3.1; 3.8).

MV-staged_design-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-staged_design-v2.text: What did each stage hand to the next?

MV-staged_design-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-staged_design-v2-ans.text: The review's blind spot became the gap the interviews went after. The interviews broke the four pillars and produced the links. The third stage tested what the interviews had raised: the first form of the fifth link in Ghent's documents, and the field's newest work with corrected strings. The fourth tested the fifth link in its final form, the holder (3.1).

MV-staged_design-v3.speaker: dr_tally
MV-staged_design-v3.text: The survey ran alongside the interviews. Doesn't that break 'each stage feeds the next'?

MV-staged_design-v3-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-staged_design-v3-ans.text: It does, and I record it as change 2 in Table 3.8. The ethics application planned the survey to follow the qualitative phase; it opened on the day of approval and ran beside the interviews on the four pillars, so it asks what the guide asked and not what the interviews found. That is why it is read for scale only (3.6; 3.8).

MQ-staged_design-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-staged_design-q1.text: When was the fourth stage, testing the holder, carried out?

MQ-staged_design-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-staged_design-q2.text: How does Table 3.1 describe the design?

MQ-staged_design-q3.speaker: sal
MQ-staged_design-q3.text: What did stage 3 read Ghent's documents for?

MG-staged_design.speaker: sal
MG-staged_design.text: The thesis never says whether it is 'mixed methods'. Use its own words: staged, qualitative at its core.

MT-stance-plain.speaker: ada
MT-stance-plain.text: A stance is the verdict a reading gives one source on one concept: it supports it, contradicts it, carries both (mixed), or says nothing on it (silent).

MT-stance-how1.speaker: ada
MT-stance-how1.text: Used for the review's cards, 'a stance being whether a paper supports a link, contradicts it, is mixed or is silent' (2.2).

MT-stance-how2.speaker: ada
MT-stance-how2.text: Used for transcripts: each of the twenty-six given a stance on each of the five concepts (3.1).

MT-stance-how3.speaker: ada
MT-stance-how3.text: Table 3.5 states, for each concept, when a transcript SUPPORTS and when it CONTRADICTS, with an example quotation (3.4).

MT-stance-how4.speaker: ada
MT-stance-how4.text: The second coding recorded, for every clause and every transcript, a stance, the exact words, their place in the transcript, and the evidence against as well as for (3.4).

MT-stance-how5.speaker: ada
MT-stance-how5.text: Counts are written supports/contradicts/mixed/silent of twenty-six, for example overlap 15/1/5/5 (1.5; Table 7.1).

MT-stance-how6.speaker: ada
MT-stance-how6.text: Qualifiers such as 'weak' or 'qualified' do not count as disagreement between readings (Table 3.6).

MT-stance-why.speaker: ada
MT-stance-why.text: The thesis defines the four values but does not say why four.

MT-stance-not.speaker: ada
MT-stance-not.text: The thesis names no alternative scheme.

MT-stance-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-stance-analogy.text: A referee with four flags for each claim: for, against, both, or nothing seen.

MV-stance-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-stance-v1.text: What does 'mixed' mean in your counts?

MV-stance-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-stance-v2.text: Give the counts for the binder.

MQ-stance-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-stance-q1.text: In '15/1/5/5' for overlap, what is the '1'?

MQ-stance-q2.speaker: ada
MQ-stance-q2.text: Under Table 3.5, when does a transcript CONTRADICT the binder concept?

MG-stance.speaker: ada
MG-stance.text: Why four values is not argued.

MT-stratified_reality-term.speaker: sal
MT-stratified_reality-term.text: Stratified reality: the empirical, the actual and the real

MT-stratified_reality-plain.speaker: sal
MT-stratified_reality-plain.text: Critical realists split reality into three layers: the real (structures and mechanisms, whether or not they are active), the actual (events that happen, seen or unseen) and the empirical (what is observed or experienced). A mechanism can exist without firing.

MT-stratified_reality-how1.speaker: sal
MT-stratified_reality-how1.text: Table 3.2, ontology row, critical realist column: 'One reality, stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real; mechanisms exist whether or not they fire (Fleetwood, 2005)'.

MT-stratified_reality-how2.speaker: sal
MT-stratified_reality-how2.text: The thesis does not map the three layers onto its own data in one place. The pieces are in 3.1: the mechanism is overlap and binding; the events are the arrangements of Appendix H and the refusals of Chapter 4; and knowledge 'comes through accounts, documents and numbers that must be read for what they can and cannot show'.

MT-stratified_reality-why.speaker: sal
MT-stratified_reality-why.text: It is given as part of the critical realist position (Fleetwood, 2005) and is not otherwise discussed. The thesis does not say how each layer bears on its design.

MT-stratified_reality-not.speaker: sal
MT-stratified_reality-not.text: Positivist ontology: 'One reality, independent of the observer and open to measurement'. Interpretivist ontology: 'Multiple realities, constructed locally and held in people's meanings' (Table 3.2).

MT-stratified_reality-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-stratified_reality-analogy.text: A magnet's pull is real even with no metal nearby (the real); a paperclip jumping to it is an event (the actual); your seeing the paperclip move is the empirical.

MX-stratified_reality-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-stratified_reality-b1.text: Critical realism sees one reality in three layers, like the floors of one building.

MX-stratified_reality-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-stratified_reality-b2.text: Top floor, the empirical: what we can observe. Interviews, documents, numbers.

MX-stratified_reality-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-stratified_reality-b3.text: Middle floor, the actual: events that happen, whether or not anyone sees them.

MX-stratified_reality-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-stratified_reality-b4.text: Ground floor, the real: mechanisms that produce events, even when they are not firing.

MX-stratified_reality-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-stratified_reality-b5.text: The thesis reads down from what was said, through events, to mechanisms.

MV-stratified_reality-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-stratified_reality-v1.text: You say reality is stratified. Where are the real, the actual and the empirical in your thesis?

MV-stratified_reality-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-stratified_reality-v1-ans.text: The real is the mechanisms, overlap and binding. The actual is the events: the arrangements of Appendix H and the refusals of Chapter 4. The empirical is what I could get at: accounts, documents and numbers, which is why each is read for what it can and cannot show (3.1; Table 3.2).

MV-stratified_reality-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-stratified_reality-v2.text: Why does it matter that a mechanism can exist without firing?

MV-stratified_reality-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-stratified_reality-v2-ans.text: Because I set the mechanism against the cases in which it should have fired and did not. Overlap can be present and still not produce a refusal, where a wall, a penalty or an owner with no stake outweighs the exposure. The mechanism is still operating; it is outweighed (3.1; 1.5).

MQ-stratified_reality-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-stratified_reality-q1.text: Which source does Table 3.2 cite for reality 'stratified into the empirical, the actual and the real'?

MQ-stratified_reality-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-stratified_reality-q2.text: In a stratified ontology, which layer holds mechanisms that may not be firing?

MG-stratified_reality.speaker: sal
MG-stratified_reality.text: The thesis states the stratified ontology but never maps the three layers onto its own evidence. Have the mapping ready.

MT-survey_instrument-term.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-term.text: The survey: a self-administered web questionnaire, read for scale

MT-survey_instrument-plain.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-plain.text: A questionnaire people fill in themselves online. Here it describes how common certain views and practices are among respondents; it does not test the thesis's links.

MT-survey_instrument-how1.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-how1.text: 'A self-administered web questionnaire of the kind Dillman, Smyth and Christian (2014) describe, a Google Form titled ‘Horizontal Collaboration in Urban Logistics’' (3.6).

MT-survey_instrument-how2.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-how2.text: Created 22 February 2024, the day the study was approved; first response that day, last on 30 April 2025; of 132 responses, 36 arrived before July 2024, 37 during the interviews (July to September 2024) and 59 from October 2024 to April 2025 (3.6).

MT-survey_instrument-how3.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-how3.text: The questions are the author's own, built on the four pillars; they 'ask what the interview guide asked, not what the interviews went on to find': nothing on market overlap, on what is pooled and withheld, on who can change how deliveries run, or on hours set by a city (3.6).

MT-survey_instrument-how4.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-how4.text: The draft of 19 February 2024 went to the ethics committee (Appendix C.4); the supervisors approved the final questions; the final form keeps the draft's thirteen questions in order and largely in its words, adds a consent item, and revises some answer lists (3.6).

MT-survey_instrument-how5.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-how5.text: Table 3.7 gives every item in the words respondents saw, its answer form and the number answering (3.6).

MT-survey_instrument-how6.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-how6.text: It records 'what organisations say matters and what they say they use, which is report and not observed conduct' (3.6).

MT-survey_instrument-why.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-why.text: 'This thesis uses it for scale' (3.6); it is 'used here to give scale to what the interviews heard of trust, not to measure the industry' (3.6). It asks about the pillars because it opened on the day of approval on the draft's questions, before the interviews produced the links (3.8, change 2).

MT-survey_instrument-not.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-not.text: The survey the ethics application planned: built on the qualitative phase's findings and analysed by correlation and regression (3.8; Appendix C.1).

MT-survey_instrument-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-survey_instrument-analogy.text: A show of hands at a trade conference: it tells you what the room says, not what each firm actually does back at the depot.

MV-survey_instrument-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-survey_instrument-v2.text: Why wasn't the survey built on your five links?

MQ-survey_instrument-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-survey_instrument-q1.text: Over what period did the survey run?

MQ-survey_instrument-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-survey_instrument-q2.text: Which of these did the survey NOT ask?

MT-systematic_review-plain.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-plain.text: A literature review run to a written protocol: a stated search, stated criteria and a logged decision for each record, so others can repeat it and see what was left out and why.

MT-systematic_review-how1.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-how1.text: The 2023 review: one search string to six databases on 1 September 2022; 860 records reduced in five stages to forty-nine studies; screened by the author; logged in the 2023 screening log (2.1; Table 3.3; Appendix E).

MT-systematic_review-how2.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-how2.text: The 2026 update: six strings in OpenAlex on 16 September 2026; 1,535 records to 241 papers (2.2; Table 3.3).

MT-systematic_review-how3.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-how3.text: 'Like the 2023 review, the update followed Tranfield, Denyer and Smart (2003) and reports to the PRISMA 2020 standard (Page et al., 2021)' (3.2).

MT-systematic_review-how4.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-how4.text: The update was screened and carded in three steps: written inclusion criteria applied at title and abstract; a second pass on every doubtful record with its abstract fetched; a reading card for every included paper, quotations located to the page wherever the full text was carded (3.2).

MT-systematic_review-how5.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-how5.text: Who screened: in 2023 'the author'; in 2026 'the author's written criteria applied to every record, each decision logged with its reason; the included set verified by the author' (Table 3.3).

MT-systematic_review-how6.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-how6.text: Every screening decision and card is logged with its reason and source in Appendix E, and both runs can be repeated from the strings (3.7).

MT-systematic_review-why.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-why.text: Tranfield, Denyer and Smart's requirement 'that a review be transparent and reproducible' (3.2), and the criterion the update 'could not do without', 'that a reader be able to run the search again' (3.2).

MT-systematic_review-not.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-not.text: For the rules and the locker networks the thesis uses a systematised review instead (Grant and Booth, 2009), a lighter form (3.5).

MT-systematic_review-analogy.speaker: ada
MT-systematic_review-analogy.text: An audited stocktake: every item counted in or out is logged with its reason, so anyone can run the count again.

MV-systematic_review-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-systematic_review-v2.text: What standard does the review report to?

MQ-systematic_review-q1.speaker: ada
MQ-systematic_review-q1.text: Which methodological source do both runs of the review follow?

MQ-systematic_review-q2.speaker: ada
MQ-systematic_review-q2.text: Where are the full logs of both runs?

MG-systematic_review.speaker: ada
MG-systematic_review.text: The thesis does not say who, or what tool, applied the written criteria to the 1,535 records in 2026; it says the criteria were the author's, every decision was logged, and the author verified the set. Expect the question and answer in those words.

MT-systematised_review-term.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-term.text: Systematised review (the rules and the locker networks)

MT-systematised_review-plain.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-plain.text: A review that records its searches, sources, dates and inclusion rules so it can be repeated, without every element of a full systematic review.

MT-systematised_review-how1.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-how1.text: Both the rules and the locker networks were gathered 'by a systematised review in the sense Grant and Booth give the term (2009, p. 95), a search that records its strings, sources, dates and inclusion rules so that it can be repeated' (3.5).

MT-systematised_review-how2.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-how2.text: Every search was run in October 2026; primary legal texts and public bodies' reports first, peer-reviewed studies next, press and industry sources only for dated events (3.5).

MT-systematised_review-how3.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-how3.text: Inclusion rules in Appendix M; the full log 'is held by the author and available on request' (3.5; 3.7).

MT-systematised_review-how4.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-how4.text: Rules read: the German postal law and its explanatory memorandum, a Swiss city's report, an Austrian ministry's guide, a European programme's framework, the Belgian postal regulator's public inquiry, the European postal regulators' report on access, and, through the press, one German city's funding rule; each read for whether it defines a neutral point by who may use it or by who holds it, and whether it looks again when control changes (3.5).

MT-systematised_review-how5.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-how5.text: Finding: 'No rule, statute or study found looks again at a point when control of it changes' (5.2).

MT-systematised_review-why.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-why.text: The thesis defines the form (a search recorded so it can be repeated) but does not say why a systematised rather than a full systematic review was run for this evidence.

MT-systematised_review-not.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-not.text: A full systematic review, as used for the literature (3.2), is not used here; the thesis does not compare them.

MT-systematised_review-analogy.speaker: lockie
MT-systematised_review-analogy.text: A logged survey of every bridge on a river, recording where you looked and what counted, without the full engineering audit of each one.

MV-systematised_review-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-systematised_review-v1.text: Why a systematised review for the rules and lockers, not a full systematic review?

MV-systematised_review-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-systematised_review-v2.text: Your search log isn't in the appendices. Why?

MQ-systematised_review-q1.speaker: lockie
MQ-systematised_review-q1.text: Whose definition of a systematised review does 3.5 use?

MQ-systematised_review-q2.speaker: lockie
MQ-systematised_review-q2.text: In the systematised review, which sources were used only for dated events?

MG-systematised_review.speaker: lockie
MG-systematised_review.text: Why systematised rather than systematic is not argued, and the full search log is not appended.

MT-thematic_analysis-term.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-term.text: Thematic analysis (Braun and Clarke) and the first coding

MT-thematic_analysis-plain.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-plain.text: Reading qualitative data closely, labelling passages with codes, and grouping the codes into themes that describe patterns across the data.

MT-thematic_analysis-how1.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-how1.text: 'The twenty-six transcripts were coded three times, in the thematic manner Braun and Clarke (2006) describe, and the order matters, because each coding was made to test the one before it' (3.4).

MT-thematic_analysis-how2.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-how2.text: The first coding was made by the author in 2024 and 2025, after the interviews, under the guide's four pillar headings (3.4).

MT-thematic_analysis-how3.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-how3.text: It is 'where the pillars broke': trust appeared only as something borrowed from outside the parties; efficiency as the driver participants named and compulsion as the one that moved them; innovation as a facilitator; sustainability as a by-product (3.4).

MT-thematic_analysis-how4.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-how4.text: From it the author wrote the working claim of 2026: the last mile is a brand asset; size sorts willingness; working arrangements run on substitutes for trust; power sits with shippers and cities; time can do what pooling was asked to (3.4).

MT-thematic_analysis-how5.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-how5.text: The survey's open answers were also coded inductively in Braun and Clarke's manner, into six themes and a code for answers with nothing of substance (3.6).

MT-thematic_analysis-why.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-why.text: The thesis does not say why it chose thematic analysis over other qualitative approaches; it says each coding was made to test the one before (3.4).

MT-thematic_analysis-not.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-not.text: The thesis names no alternative qualitative method.

MT-thematic_analysis-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-thematic_analysis-analogy.text: Sorting a heap of letters into piles by what they are about, then noticing the piles you expected don't fit and new piles forming.

MV-thematic_analysis-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-thematic_analysis-v1.text: What did the first coding produce?

MQ-thematic_analysis-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-thematic_analysis-q1.text: Under which headings was the first coding made?

MQ-thematic_analysis-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-thematic_analysis-q2.text: Which of these was a clause of the working claim of 2026?

MG-thematic_analysis.speaker: sam
MG-thematic_analysis.text: Why thematic analysis rather than another approach is not argued.

MT-theory_building-plain.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-plain.text: Research that develops explanations and propositions from cases rather than testing ready-made hypotheses. Testing the propositions is left for later work.

MT-theory_building-how1.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-how1.text: The abstract calls the design 'critical realist, theory-building'.

MT-theory_building-how2.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-how2.text: 'Because it takes a critical realist view, this research builds theory rather than testing it' (3.1).

MT-theory_building-how3.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-how3.text: 'Theory is developed here, not tested as hypotheses against measurement: the framework of 2.7 was drawn from the interviews, its fifth link from the interviews read again beside the locker networks and the rules, and it is offered in Chapter 7 as propositions, each of two variables, for others to test' (3.1).

MT-theory_building-how4.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-how4.text: Statistical tests appear in the later stages, but the locker difference 'fits the link but does not test it' (1.5).

MT-theory_building-how5.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-how5.text: 'Because the design was theory-building, the contribution is offered as propositions rather than as tested hypotheses, each a single statement relating two variables, under the conditions it names, that others may test in their own context' (7.2).

MT-theory_building-why.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-why.text: It follows from the paradigm: 'Because it takes a critical realist view, this research builds theory rather than testing it' (3.1).

MT-theory_building-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-theory_building-analogy.text: Drawing the first reliable chart of a coastline from sailors' logs; sounding every bay is the next voyage.

MV-theory_building-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-theory_building-v1.text: You ran Fisher's exact test and a permutation test. How is this theory-building?

MQ-theory_building-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-theory_building-q1.text: Because the design was theory-building, how is the contribution offered?

MQ-theory_building-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-theory_building-q2.text: From what was the fifth link drawn?

MT-three_codings-term.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-term.text: The three codings of the transcripts

MT-three_codings-plain.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-plain.text: The transcripts were coded three times, each coding built to test the one before it, so the framework can be shown to have come from the data.

MT-three_codings-how1.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-how1.text: First coding (2024 and 2025, by the author): under the four pillar headings; the pillars broke; the working claim of 2026 was written from it (3.4).

MT-three_codings-how2.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-how2.text: Second coding (September 2026): a codebook coding (Miles, Huberman and Saldaña, 2014) built to test the working claim, not Table 3.5; transcripts pseudonymised first; coded in two halves, A1 to A13 and B1 to B13, each read in full without the notes of the first coding; for every clause and transcript it recorded a stance, the exact words, their place and the evidence against as well as for (3.4).

MT-three_codings-how3.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-how3.text: Result: two clauses, brand and size, were not sustained; two regularities the claim had not named, overlap and the boundary of sharing, appeared; the codebook of Table 3.5 was rewritten from these results (3.4).

MT-three_codings-how4.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-how4.text: Third coding: against Table 3.5, again in two halves of thirteen, so that 'every count in Chapters 4 and 5 is a count against the concepts the thesis actually claims and not against the claim it abandoned'; each half coded a second time without sight of its first codes (3.4).

MT-three_codings-why.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-why.text: 'Each coding was made to test the one before it' (3.4). The second was made 'to test what the first had produced before anything was built on it'; the third so that counts are against the concepts actually claimed (3.4). 'A framework that emerged in that order can be shown to have emerged, and one that had been imposed could not' (1.6). The guide's headings were not used for the second coding 'because the guide's four headings were the hypothesis the data had already overturned, and coding the transcripts under them would have measured the hypothesis rather than the data' (3.4).

MT-three_codings-not.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-not.text: Coding once, or coding under the guide's headings throughout (rejected, 3.4).

MT-three_codings-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-three_codings-analogy.text: Drafting a map, sending a second surveyor out with the draft to find where it is wrong, then sending a third with the corrected map to count what lies where.

MX-three_codings-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-three_codings-b1.text: The same twenty-six transcripts were coded three times. Each coding tested the one before.

MX-three_codings-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-three_codings-b2.text: First, under the four pillars the interviews were designed around. The pillars broke.

MX-three_codings-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-three_codings-b3.text: From that reading came a working claim: brand, size, substitutes for trust, power, time.

MX-three_codings-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-three_codings-b4.text: Second, the claim was tested without the first coding's notes. Brand and size fell.

MX-three_codings-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-three_codings-b5.text: Third, every transcript was coded against the rewritten codebook, and each half read twice.

MX-three_codings-b6.speaker: marigold
MX-three_codings-b6.text: So every count is against what the thesis claims, not what it abandoned.

MV-three_codings-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-three_codings-v1.text: Why three codings rather than one?

MV-three_codings-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-three_codings-v1-ans.text: Because each tested the one before. The first, under the pillars, broke them and produced a working claim. The second tested that claim, and two clauses, brand and size, fell while overlap and the boundary of sharing appeared. The third coded every transcript against the rewritten codebook, so every count is against what I actually claim, not the claim I abandoned (3.4).

MV-three_codings-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
