MV-three_codings-v2.text: Isn't rewriting the codebook from the second coding's results circular?

MV-three_codings-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-three_codings-v2-ans.text: The third coding counts against concepts the second coding found, yes; that is the point, so that the counts are against what the thesis claims. The check against the coding itself is the second, blind reading of each half, which agreed on 112 of 130 stances, and every difference is listed (3.4; Table 3.6).

MV-three_codings-v3.speaker: dr_tally
MV-three_codings-v3.text: When was the second coding done, and against what?

MV-three_codings-v3-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-three_codings-v3-ans.text: In September 2026, against the working claim of 2026, not against Table 3.5, on pseudonymised transcripts, in two halves, each read in full without the first coding's notes (3.4).

MQ-three_codings-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-three_codings-q1.text: What was the second coding built to test?

MQ-three_codings-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-three_codings-q2.text: Which two regularities did the second coding produce that the claim had not named?

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-plain.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-plain.text: A guide to doing a doctorate with the viva in mind. It fixes the order in which a design is explained (paradigm, approach, methodology, methods) and supplies checklists for the design, the framework and the claim.

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how1.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how1.text: Chapter 3 sets its choices out 'in the order Trafford and Leshem (2008, ch. 6) recommend': the paradigm (critical realist), then the approach (retroductive), then the methodology (a design in four stages, qualitative at its core), then the methods (3.1).

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how2.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how2.text: Table 3.1 answers the six questions they put to a research design (2008, p. 91): what the research wants to discover, why, when and over what period, how, where and who (3.1).

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how3.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how3.text: The conceptual framework is tested with Berger and Patchner's three questions as they cite them (p. 85) and with the test they call critical (p. 87): unity, direction, meaning and coherence (2.7).

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how4.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how4.text: Figure 3.3 audits the whole design in the form Rose (1982) proposed, as they carry it (pp. 103-104) (3.7).

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how5.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how5.text: Every change of plan is explained, because they hold that a change of plan must be explained in the thesis (pp. 99, 104) (3.8).

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how6.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-how6.text: The contribution is claimed as 'modest in the way Trafford and Leshem (2008, p. 141) ask': each form traceable to a chapter, a count and an appendix row (7.2).

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-why.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-why.text: The thesis does not say why it adopts Trafford and Leshem as its frame. It uses their order and their tests at each point listed; the reference list gives the book's full title, 'Stepping stones to achieving your doctorate: by focusing on your viva from the start'.

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-not.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-not.text: The thesis names no alternative frame.

MT-trafford_leshem_frame-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-trafford_leshem_frame-analogy.text: A building inspector's checklist: it does not design the house, but it fixes the order in which the plans are shown and the questions each must answer.

MV-trafford_leshem_frame-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-trafford_leshem_frame-v1.text: Why is your methodology chapter ordered paradigm, approach, methodology, methods?

MV-trafford_leshem_frame-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-trafford_leshem_frame-v2.text: You call your contribution modest. What do you mean?

MQ-trafford_leshem_frame-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-trafford_leshem_frame-q1.text: In what order does Chapter 3 set out its choices?

MG-trafford_leshem_frame.speaker: sam
MG-trafford_leshem_frame.text: Why this frame and not another is not stated.

MT-translation_checking-term.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-term.text: Translation and checking the Dutch extracts

MT-translation_checking-plain.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-plain.text: When evidence is in another language, making each translation checkable: translating only what is used, checking it several ways, and printing the original beside it.

MT-translation_checking-how1.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-how1.text: Both Ghent documents are in Dutch; only the extracts used were translated (3.5).

MT-translation_checking-how2.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-how2.text: 'Each rendering was made for this thesis and checked by the author against the Dutch original, against a second translation made independently of the first, and against a dictionary; no Dutch speaker checked them, which 7.4 carries as a limit' (3.5).

MT-translation_checking-how3.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-how3.text: Appendix J sets the Dutch beside the English, 'so that the reader, not the author, has the last word on each' (7.4).

MT-translation_checking-how4.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-how4.text: The survey's four open answers in Spanish, French, German and Italian were rendered into English, and Appendix K sets each original beside its rendering (3.6).

MT-translation_checking-why.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-why.text: Meaning 'was held to the Dutch by translating only the extracts used and setting the Dutch beside the English in Appendix J so that a reader can check each rendering, which is the practice Temple and Young (2004) ask of research that crosses a language' (3.5).

MT-translation_checking-not.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-not.text: Checking by a Dutch-speaking reader, not done and stated as a limit (7.4).

MT-translation_checking-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-translation_checking-analogy.text: A bilingual menu: the original dish name sits beside the translation, so anyone who reads both can catch a mistake.

MV-translation_checking-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-translation_checking-v1.text: You don't speak Dutch. How can I trust your renderings?

MV-translation_checking-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-translation_checking-v2.text: Did you translate the whole of both plans?

MQ-translation_checking-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-translation_checking-q1.text: Which check was NOT applied to the Dutch renderings?

MQ-translation_checking-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-translation_checking-q2.text: Where can the Dutch and English be read side by side?

MT-triangulation-plain.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-plain.text: Checking a claim against different kinds of evidence. If separate sources point the same way, the claim is stronger; if one disagrees, that is reported.

MT-triangulation-how1.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-how1.text: 'The triangulation is the review, the interviews, the documents and the survey read against one another' (3.1).

MT-triangulation-how2.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-how2.text: On what binds: 95 of the 117 arrangements are bound from outside the parties, while survey respondents rate trust highly (89 of 119 at 4 or 5) and, among the 45 who said how they keep it, name formal contracts, third-party coordination and public authority support beside joint planning (4.4; 5.3).

MT-triangulation-how3.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-how3.text: On the holder: three kinds of evidence, the 117 arrangements recoded, the locker networks and the rules (1.5).

MT-triangulation-how4.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-how4.text: On power: the update's count rests partly on a decision rule that assumes the claim, so it is tested instead on the interviews and on who began the 117 arrangements (2.2; 4.5).

MT-triangulation-how5.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-how5.text: The survey 'is set beside them, not in their place' (3.6).

MT-triangulation-why.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-why.text: It is one of Wynn and Williams's principles (3.1). The thesis gives no further reason.

MT-triangulation-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-triangulation-analogy.text: Fixing a position from three landmarks rather than one: any single bearing can be off, but where three lines cross the fix can be trusted.

MX-triangulation-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-triangulation-b1.text: One source can mislead. Triangulation asks several kinds of evidence the same question.

MX-triangulation-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-triangulation-b2.text: Here there are four: the review, the interviews, the documents and the survey.

MX-triangulation-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-triangulation-b3.text: Each casts a line towards the same claim: what holds rivals together.

MX-triangulation-b4.speaker: marigold
MX-triangulation-b4.text: Where lines cross, confidence grows. Where one bends away, it is reported, not hidden.

MX-triangulation-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-triangulation-b5.text: The survey sits beside the 117 arrangements, never in their place.

MV-triangulation-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-triangulation-v1.text: Your survey tests no link. How can it triangulate?

MV-triangulation-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-triangulation-v1-ans.text: It sits beside the links rather than testing them. It shows what organisations say about trust next to what they report using to keep it: 89 of 119 rate trust at 4 or 5, and among the 45 who said how they keep it, formal contracts, third-party coordination and public authority support are named beside joint planning. What binds is shown by the 117 arrangements, 95 of them bound from outside (3.6; 5.3; 4.4).

MV-triangulation-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-triangulation-v2.text: Give an example where your sources pull in different directions.

MV-triangulation-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-triangulation-v2-ans.text: Trust. Survey respondents rate it highly; the arrangements show 95 of 117 bound from outside the parties and six by their own trust. I report both, and read the survey as what people say matters and what they say they use, not as what binds (5.3; 4.4).

MQ-triangulation-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-triangulation-q1.text: Which four sources does 3.1 name as triangulated?

MQ-triangulation-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-triangulation-q2.text: How does 3.6 position the survey against the 117 arrangements?

MT-two_halves-term.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-term.text: Coding in two halves (A1 to A13 and B1 to B13)

MT-two_halves-plain.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-plain.text: Splitting the transcripts into two sets and coding each separately, so a misreading in one set is less likely to spread to the whole.

MT-two_halves-how1.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-how1.text: The codes A1 to A13 and B1 to B13 follow the order the transcripts were filed and divided into two halves (3.3).

MT-two_halves-how2.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-how2.text: The second coding read each half in full against the working claim, separately (3.4).

MT-two_halves-how3.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-how3.text: The third coding was 'again made in two halves of thirteen transcripts each'; 'because the two halves are different transcripts, their counts are summed, not compared' (3.4).

MT-two_halves-how4.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-how4.text: Each half was then coded a second time for the agreement check: A half 53 of 65, B half 59 of 65 (3.4; Table 3.6).

MT-two_halves-why.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-why.text: In the second coding, 'the halves were coded separately so that a systematic misreading in either would show as a difference between the halves' (3.4).

MT-two_halves-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-two_halves-analogy.text: Two bakers each making half the batch from the same recipe: if one loaf tastes off, you know which half to check.

MV-two_halves-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-two_halves-v1.text: Why split the transcripts into halves?

MV-two_halves-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-two_halves-v2.text: If the halves are different transcripts, how would a difference between them reveal a misreading?

MQ-two_halves-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-two_halves-q1.text: In the third coding, how are the two halves' counts combined?

MQ-two_halves-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-two_halves-q2.text: What did the A half's two readings agree on?

MG-two_halves.speaker: sam
MG-two_halves.text: The thesis says the halves were split so a misreading would show as a difference between them, but in the third coding the halves are summed, not compared, and it does not say how a real difference between two sets of transcripts would be told apart from a misreading.

MT-two_readings-term.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-term.text: The second reading, blind to the first

MT-two_readings-plain.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-plain.text: Coding the same material a second time without seeing the first set of codes, then comparing the two, to check that the codebook can be applied consistently.

MT-two_readings-how1.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-how1.text: The third coding's check was 'the agreement that O'Connor and Joffe (2020) recommend for codebook work, obtained by coding each half a second time against the same codebook without sight of its first codes' (3.4).

MT-two_readings-how2.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-how2.text: 'Each coding of a half was made from the transcripts and Table 3.5 alone, to the author's written criteria of 3.2' (3.4).

MT-two_readings-how3.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-how3.text: Result: 112 of 130 stances read the same way twice, 86 per cent; A half 53 of 65, B half 59 of 65 (3.4; Table 3.6).

MT-two_readings-how4.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-how4.text: The eighteen differences fall on twelve transcripts; five of the eighteen on two transcripts, B8 and B10 (Table 3.6 note).

MT-two_readings-how5.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-how5.text: 'Where the readings differed Chapter 4 gives both': Table 4.9 for the first four concepts, Chapter 5 for time (3.4; 4.1).

MT-two_readings-how6.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-how6.text: The second reading moved numbers at the margins, not their direction: overlap 15 to 12 supporting (mixed 5 to 7); boundary 16 to 21 (mixed 6 to 2); binds 24 to 25; power 18 to 16 (mixed 5 to 8); time 5 to 6 (4.1).

MT-two_readings-why.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-why.text: It is the agreement O'Connor and Joffe recommend for codebook work (3.4); it is also part of the answer to the exposure 'that the author interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim the later codings tested' (3.7).

MT-two_readings-not.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-not.text: A chance-corrected coefficient for this check (see raw agreement).

MT-two_readings-analogy.speaker: sal
MT-two_readings-analogy.text: Re-marking a pile of essays a month later with the first marks hidden, then laying both sets of marks side by side.

MX-two_readings-b1.speaker: marigold
MX-two_readings-b1.text: A codebook is only useful if it gives the same answer twice.

MX-two_readings-b2.speaker: marigold
MX-two_readings-b2.text: Each half was coded, then coded again with the first codes hidden.

MX-two_readings-b3.speaker: marigold
MX-two_readings-b3.text: Then the two readings were laid side by side.

MX-two_readings-b5.speaker: marigold
MX-two_readings-b5.text: Every one of the eighteen differences is listed, and both readings reported.

MV-two_readings-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-two_readings-v1.text: What changed when each half was read a second time?

MV-two_readings-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-two_readings-v1-ans.text: The numbers moved at the margins but not their direction. Overlap went from fifteen supporting to twelve, with mixed rising from five to seven; the boundary from sixteen to twenty-one; what binds from twenty-four to twenty-five; power from eighteen to sixteen; time from five to six. Wherever the readings differ, Chapter 4 gives both (4.1; Table 4.9).

MV-two_readings-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-two_readings-v2-ans.text: Each reading of a half was made from the transcripts and Table 3.5 alone, without sight of the other reading's codes, to my written criteria, and every decision was logged and checked by me (3.4; 3.2).

MQ-two_readings-q1.speaker: sal
MQ-two_readings-q1.text: After the second reading, how many transcripts supported overlap?

MQ-two_readings-q2.speaker: sal
MQ-two_readings-q2.text: On which two transcripts do five of the eighteen differences fall?

MG-two_readings.speaker: sal
MG-two_readings.text: The thesis does not name who made each reading; it says each was made from the transcripts and the codebook alone, to the author's written criteria, and checked by the author. Answer in those words.

MT-unit_of_analysis-term.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-term.text: Unit of analysis: the collaborative arrangement

MT-unit_of_analysis-plain.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-plain.text: The unit of analysis is the thing a study's findings are about, its 'case'. It decides what is counted and compared.

MT-unit_of_analysis-how1.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-how1.text: 'The collaborative arrangement: each observed or attempted collaboration, described by whether the parties' markets overlapped, what was shared, and what bound it' (1.4).

MT-unit_of_analysis-how2.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-how2.text: It is 'the case in Yin's (2018) sense, the thing the research question is about' (3.1).

MT-unit_of_analysis-how3.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-how3.text: Each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration a participant described is one row of Appendix H, coded for overlap, what was pooled and withheld, what bound it, who began it, its status at interview and whether it used time; in October 2026 each row was coded again for the meeting point, its holder, whether the holder sells delivery to the parties' customers and whether its co-users are rivals (3.1).

MT-unit_of_analysis-how4.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-how4.text: Operators and documents are the sources; the survey is read by organisation and for scale only (1.4).

MT-unit_of_analysis-how5.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-how5.text: Each case is limited 'to what the participant described, and no further', the discipline Miles, Huberman and Saldaña (2014) ask for, which lets the 117 rows be read beside the 241 papers (unit: the paper) and Ghent's permit categories (unit: the class of operator) (3.1).

MT-unit_of_analysis-why.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-why.text: 'Because a finding about willingness concerns a pair of markets and a finding about binding concerns an arrangement, and neither is a property of a firm' (1.4).

MT-unit_of_analysis-not.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-not.text: The firm: 'neither is a property of a firm' (1.4).

MT-unit_of_analysis-analogy.speaker: vera
MT-unit_of_analysis-analogy.text: Studying marriages rather than spouses: whether a marriage lasts is a property of the pair and what holds it, not of either person alone.

MV-unit_of_analysis-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-unit_of_analysis-v1.text: If the unit is the arrangement, why do you count transcripts at all?

MV-unit_of_analysis-v1-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-unit_of_analysis-v1-ans.text: Because there are two units of counting and I keep them apart. Stances are counted by transcript, one participant's testimony each; arrangements by row of Appendix H. A count of transcripts is a count of accounts; a count of rows is a count of accounts of arrangements (3.1; 3.4).

MV-unit_of_analysis-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-unit_of_analysis-v2.text: How did you bound the case?

MV-unit_of_analysis-v2-ans.speaker: marigold
MV-unit_of_analysis-v2-ans.text: By what the participant described and no further, as Miles, Huberman and Saldaña ask. Each operating, ended, piloted or concretely proposed collaboration a participant described is one row. That is what lets the 117 rows sit beside the 241 papers and Ghent's permit categories, each with its own unit (3.1).

MQ-unit_of_analysis-q1.speaker: vera
MQ-unit_of_analysis-q1.text: What is the thesis's unit of analysis?

MQ-unit_of_analysis-q2.speaker: vera
MQ-unit_of_analysis-q2.text: Which collaborations count as a row of Appendix H?

MT-units_of_counting-term.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-term.text: Two units of counting: the transcript and the row (and the row rule)

MT-units_of_counting-plain.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-plain.text: When a study counts, it must say what one unit is. Here one transcript (one participant's testimony) and one row (one account of one arrangement) are counted separately and never mixed.

MT-units_of_counting-how1.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-how1.text: Transcript: each of the twenty-six read as a whole and given a stance on each of the five concepts (supports, contradicts, mixed, silent), so 'a count of transcripts is a count of accounts' (3.1).

MT-units_of_counting-how2.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-how2.text: Every count of stances is 'a count of transcripts, not of mentions' (4.1).

MT-units_of_counting-how3.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-how3.text: Row: one row of Appendix H per description of an arrangement. The row rule: 'a scheme described by two participants becomes two rows, each pointing to the other', so 'a count of rows is therefore a count of accounts of arrangements, not of separate arrangements' (3.1).

MT-units_of_counting-how4.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-how4.text: A half: a first listing of 39 items (accounts of 37 arrangements); the appendix gives those 39 rows and adds 17 the listing left out, 56 rows, holding between 51 and 52 unique schemes once two repeated descriptions are merged. B half: 61 items, 61 rows. Total: 117 (3.4).

MT-units_of_counting-how5.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-how5.text: Two further units for the fifth link: the locker network counted by ownership period (47 periods of 43 networks) and the rule, read for how it defines a neutral point (3.1).

MT-units_of_counting-why.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-why.text: Transcripts: 'because a transcript is one participant's testimony and a participant who said a thing three times said it once' (3.4). Rows: 'because what is counted is the description, not the scheme' (3.1).

MT-units_of_counting-analogy.speaker: sam
MT-units_of_counting-analogy.text: Counting witnesses versus counting statements about each incident: two witnesses describing the same crash give two statements, and the report says so.

MV-units_of_counting-v1.speaker: dr_tally
MV-units_of_counting-v1.text: Why is 117 not the number of arrangements?

MV-units_of_counting-v2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
MV-units_of_counting-v2.text: Why count by transcript rather than by mention?

MQ-units_of_counting-q1.speaker: sam
MQ-units_of_counting-q1.text: A scheme described by two participants becomes how many rows of Appendix H?

MQ-units_of_counting-q2.speaker: sam
MQ-units_of_counting-q2.text: How many rows does the A half contribute to Appendix H?

MT-update_2026-plain.speaker: ada
MT-update_2026-plain.text: An update runs a review again later, here with corrected search terms, to reach work the first search could not see.

MT-update_2026-how1.speaker: ada
MT-update_2026-how1.text: Run 16 September 2026 in OpenAlex's title-and-abstract field, through its public interface; six strings, the original plus five corrected (Table 3.3).

MT-update_2026-how2.speaker: ada
MT-update_2026-how2.text: Document types: the written types of 2023, applied to the type the index records, so conference papers, dissertations and preprints were removed; two items recorded as articles, a capstone project and a peer-reviewed conference abstract, remain (Table 3.3).

MT-update_2026-how3.speaker: ada
MT-update_2026-how3.text: Dates: 2018 onwards; earlier papers kept only if cited thirty times or more (Table 3.3).

MT-update_2026-how4.speaker: ada
MT-update_2026-how4.text: 1,535 identified; 1,023 of eligible type; 254 relevant on title and abstract (208 first pass; 46 of 150 doubtful records at a second pass with abstracts fetched); 242 records, 241 papers (Table 3.3).

MT-update_2026-how5.speaker: ada
MT-update_2026-how5.text: Nine of the 241 were among the forty-nine; a tenth had reached the 2023 full-text stage and been set aside (2.2).

MT-update_2026-why.speaker: ada
MT-update_2026-why.text: The 2022 string 'was written for the last mile, and its reach could be tested before any new search was run'; the update 'was built to reach the literature the twelve belong to' (2.2). Three deliberate differences (3.2): the corrected strings name the subject; one index replaced four; and earlier papers were kept by a stated rule. On the rule: 'Tranfield, Denyer and Smart's (2003) requirement that a review be transparent and reproducible is better met by a threshold anyone can apply than by selection by judgement' (3.2). The second pass exists because OpenAlex carries fewer abstracts per article (3.2). The thesis does not say why the threshold is thirty rather than another number.

AF-E-f7.text: The closest surviving list to the 72 is the EndNote export of 27 January 2023: 79 records, the 49 plus 30 others.

AF-E-f8.speaker: marigold
AF-E-f8.text: The 2026 re-run of the full-text stage assessed 31 papers twice: 29 exclusions stand (25 off-topic, 3 outside urban last mile, 1 on publication type) and 2 papers meet the criteria; subject agreement 30 of 31.

AF-E-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-E-f9.text: The update's six strings, run on OpenAlex on 16 September 2026, returned 1,535 unique records; 1,023 were of an eligible type; 254 were relevant on title and abstract (208 at first pass plus 46 of 150 doubtful); the thirty-citation rule left 242 records, which are 241 papers.

AF-E-f10.speaker: marigold
AF-E-f10.text: The 241 by type: models or simulations 124 (51%), empirical 56, reviews 28, conceptual 23, reports 9, and one whose type could not be established.

AF-E-f11.speaker: marigold
AF-E-f11.text: 128 of the 241 (53%) name no initiator; where one is named, public bodies begin 45, carriers 29, platforms 20 and shippers or receivers 13.

AF-E-f12.speaker: marigold

EQ-app-E-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-E-eq1.text: Your record doesn't list the 72 papers or say why 23 were dropped. How can we trust the 49?

MA-app-E-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-E-eq1.text: The 2023 record does have gaps, and I set them out myself in E.2.9. The screening log gives 72 as a count and nothing else. The manuscript I submitted to MDPI Future Transportation in March 2023 gives the same counts and four topic labels for what was dropped, crowd-shipping, travelling salesman problems, bicycle deliveries and public transport sharing, but no list of the 72 and no reason per paper. So in 2026 I re-ran that stage: every paper that could have been among the 23, the 30 in the January 2023 EndNote export that aren't in the 49, plus Kanter, coded twice against the 2023 criteria. Twenty-nine exclusions stand, two papers meet the criteria, and neither is a kind the 49 lack. Agreement on subject was 30 of 31, alpha .91 (E.2.10).

EQ-app-E-eq2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-E-eq2.text: Why do you report 860 records when the stages start from 662?

MA-app-E-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-E-eq2.text: 860 is the 662 records plus the 198 published before 2018. The eight pre-2018 papers I added by hand sit in both, under 'Extra' in the 662 and in the pre-2018 column, so 860 counts them twice. I keep 860 because it's the figure the 2023 manuscript reports, and I explain the double count in E.2.4, in 2.1 and in Table 3.3.

EQ-app-E-eq3.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-E-eq3.text: Why did you switch from four databases to OpenAlex for the update?

MA-app-E-eq3.speaker: marigold
MA-app-E-eq3.text: Reproducibility. The criterion I couldn't do without was that a reader can run the search again. A public index through a public interface allows that for anyone; four databases behind institutional logins allow it only for subscribers. On Culbert and colleagues' comparison OpenAlex's coverage is comparable to Web of Science and Scopus, though it carries fewer abstracts, so every doubtful record got a second pass with its abstract fetched (3.2).

EQ-app-E-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-E-eq4.text: Can you really compare 241 papers with 49 studies?

MA-app-E-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-E-eq4.text: Only with care, and I say which kind each is every time they stand together. The 49 were included after full-text reading; the 241 were kept after title-and-abstract screening and the thirty-citation rule, and 170 of them were then read in full. So it's a looser set beside a stricter one (2.2, 3.2).

EQ-app-E-eq5.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-E-eq5.text: Your counts on 'where the power sits' look circular.

MA-app-E-eq5.speaker: marigold
MA-app-E-eq5.text: They are, in part, and I say so. Thirty-eight of the 241 verdicts on power were assigned by a rule that counts shippers, receivers, cities or a neutral orchestrator as support and carriers as against, which is the thesis's own claim. So that count only shows whom the field assumes decides. Whether power really sits there is tested in 4.5, with the interviews and who began the 117 arrangements (2.2; E.3.2.1).

EQ-app-E-eq6.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-E-eq6.text: Why did the 2022 string miss the horizontal-collaboration literature?

MA-app-E-eq6.speaker: marigold
MA-app-E-eq6.text: Because it requires 'last mile'. A paper that says 'horizontal collaboration' but not 'last mile' is invisible to it. Run again in OpenAlex it returns none of the twelve papers in Appendix F, and only 39 of the 231 update papers that weren't in the 2023 review; 192 fall outside its terms altogether (2.2).

AF-F-f2.speaker: marigold
AF-F-f2.text: The other eleven were not screened in 2023.

AF-F-f5.text: Run again in OpenAlex, the 2022 string returns none of the twelve.

AF-F-f8.speaker: marigold
AF-F-f8.text: Frisk and colleagues found a saving of 8.9 per cent against each company planning alone, and up to 14% against transport actually run.

AF-F-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-F-f9.text: In Eirinakis and colleagues' load exchange, the share of loads matched rose from 9.7 per cent of 318 to 21.4 per cent of 373.

EQ-app-F-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-F-eq1.text: How did you choose these twelve? Isn't that cherry-picking?

MA-app-F-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-F-eq1.text: They're the papers inside the field's own citation trail on horizontal collaboration, named in the evidence I assembled for the research gap on 15 September 2026. They're not offered as a sample; they're a test of the 2022 string's reach, and run again in OpenAlex it finds none of them. The update itself was then run systematically, with six strings (E.2.8; 2.2).

EQ-app-F-eq2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-F-eq2.text: Three of them aren't about freight. Why include them?

MA-app-F-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-F-eq2.text: Each names horizontal collaboration, coordination or coopetition in its title, but none is about freight, so a last-mile string couldn't be expected to find them. The case that the 2022 string missed the collaboration literature rests on the other nine. I read the three because each tests, outside freight, a condition the freight papers raise (2.2).

EQ-app-F-eq3.speaker: dr_tally

EQ-app-F-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-F-eq4.text: What did these papers add to your argument?

MA-app-F-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-F-eq4.text: Three of the field's oldest instruments: cost allocation, the trustee device and the typologies. Frisk's authors call for an independent organisation to run the bartering; in Basso's account the three-company trial worked while a third party with no interest in any of the companies was involved, and ended when none could be found (2.2).

AF-I-f2.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f2.text: The working claim tested: carriers refuse because the last mile is a brand asset, and small operators collaborate freely while large branded ones refuse.

AF-I-f3.speaker: marigold

AF-I-f4.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f4.text: Barriers reported in the B half, by frequency: operating data as a competitive asset 8 of 13, market overlap 6, cost with no business model after subsidy 6, service control and liability 4; visibility three times.

AF-I-f5.speaker: marigold

AF-I-f6.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f6.text: Third coding over all 26, first reading (supports / contradicts / mixed / silent): overlap 15/1/5/5; boundary 16/1/6/3; what binds 24/0/1/1; power 18/0/5/3; time 5/0/2/19. The second reading gives overlap 12/0/7/7, boundary 21/0/2/3, what binds 25/0/1/0, power 16/0/8/2, time 6/0/1/19.

AF-I-f7.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f7.text: Agreement between first and second readings: 53 of 65 stances on A1-A13, 59 of 65 on B1-B13, 112 of 130 overall (86 per cent).

AF-I-f8.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f8.text: The eighteen differences fall on twelve transcripts; B8 and B10 carry five of them, and five of the A half's twelve fall on the boundary concept.

AF-I-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f9.text: Brand was put by the interviewer in five interviews and declined in all five, and raised unprompted by participants in eight.

AF-I-f10.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f10.text: File 1's methodological cautions: the brand frame was introduced by the interviewer; positions were relayed between interviews; A9 is substantially incomplete; A5's 'successes' are proposals; A6's case was not yet running.

AF-I-f11.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f11.text: The keyword sweep for brand words was corrected: 'livery' matched inside 'delivery', giving more than sixty false hits.

AF-I-f12.speaker: marigold
AF-I-f12.text: B10 and B11 lie outside urban last-mile logistics; excluding them leaves eleven transcripts in the B half.

EQ-app-I-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-I-eq1.text: You interviewed, coded first and wrote the claim. Isn't the analysis just you agreeing with yourself?

MA-app-I-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-I-eq1.text: That's the exposure no procedure removes, and I name it in 3.7. What I did about it: the second and third codings were made from the transcripts alone, without the notes of the first; each had to record the evidence against as well as for; each half was read a second time without sight of its first codes; and the second coding threw out two of my own clauses, brand and size.

EQ-app-I-eq2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-I-eq2.text: Why report raw agreement rather than kappa?

MA-app-I-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-I-eq2.text: With four possible stances, thirteen transcripts a half and a fifth concept where silence dominates, a coefficient would say less than the list of the eighteen differences itself. So I give 112 of 130, 86 per cent, and every difference by concept and transcript in Table 3.6. For the 117 arrangements, where the unit and the numbers suit it, I use Krippendorff's alpha.

EQ-app-I-eq3.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-I-eq3.text: Did you plant the brand idea in your participants' heads?

MA-app-I-eq3.speaker: marigold
MA-app-I-eq3.text: I raised it in five interviews and it was declined in all five; participants raised it unprompted in eight. I count the five as declined, not as support, and the coding files list separately every theme I introduced or relayed, so none of it is counted as the participant's view.

EQ-app-I-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-I-eq4.text: Some transcripts are poor. Which ones, and what did you do?

MA-app-I-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-I-eq4.text: A9 is substantially incomplete and its answers were typed in afterwards, so I read it as low confidence throughout. A5 is eight minutes of prepared answers. B8 has phone audio and limited English. B10 and B11 turned out to lie outside the domain: they stay in every count of twenty-six, both codings mark them silent on most concepts, and no finding rests on them alone (3.7; 4.1).

EQ-app-I-eq5.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-I-eq5.text: What did the second coding actually change?

MA-app-I-eq5.speaker: marigold
MA-app-I-eq5.text: It didn't sustain two clauses of my working claim, brand and size, and it found two regularities the claim hadn't named: overlap and the boundary of sharing. The codebook of Table 3.5 was rewritten from those results, and the third coding was made against it (3.4).

AF-L-f1.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f1.text: The condition tested is that collaboration between overlapping operators runs only when the saving plus the penalty for staying out at least equals the exposure of the customer relationship plus the cost of the wall.

AF-L-f2.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f2.text: Version 2 of the codebook followed a pilot on ten rows (H1-1 to H1-5 and H2-1 to H2-5), after which seven changes were made.

AF-L-f3.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f3.text: Version 3 (28 October 2026) adds the holder of the shared point, in six classes: receiver, no-stake third party, helper, public body, rival party, joint.

AF-L-f4.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f4.text: Version-2 agreement: market commonality .84, footprint .84, outcome .87 (firm); wall .76 (tentative); penalty .54, stage .59, flows .55, what crosses .65 (below the bar).

AF-L-f5.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f5.text: The initiator, copied from Appendix H and re-checked in each pass, agreed in 98 of 117 rows.

AF-L-f6.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f6.text: Version-3 agreement: holder class .88 (106/117), sells delivery .87, co-users rivals .85, neutral holder .84 (107/117); 35 disagreeing codes across 24 rows, all settled.

AF-L-f7.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f7.text: Krippendorff's bars: .800 for firm conclusions, .667 for tentative ones.

AF-L-f8.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f8.text: Among rivals not far from the customer, arrangements with a wall or a penalty were running in 11 of 13 (pass C) and 11 of 12 (pass D); with neither and normal flows, in 3 of 8 and 2 of 8.

AF-L-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f9.text: Where something actually crosses, 7 of 8 (pass C) and 8 of 9 (pass D) run with a wall or a penalty; the one running exception with neither is H2-56, two bike couriers' joint bid.

AF-L-f10.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f10.text: Rule 1a (a trustee that runs the scheme is the holder; the operator it hires is a helper) was added after the results were seen; with it the holder condition reaches 9 of 10 running rows (0.90), without it 6 of 7 (0.86).

AF-L-f11.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f11.text: Rule 1a changes three rows, the one trustee-run shipper network: H1-11, H1-17 and H1-37.

AF-L-f12.speaker: marigold
AF-L-f12.text: No row was coded 'receiver' as holder.

EQ-app-L-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-L-eq1.text: Rule 1a was added after you saw the results. Isn't that data dredging?

MA-app-L-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-L-eq1.text: It was added after the results, and I say so plainly in L.1, 3.7, 4.4 and 7.4. The reason was mechanical: version 3 moved the trustee out of the wall code and into the holder code, but the tie-break rule then sent the holder to the hired operator in the three rows of the one trustee-run shipper network, so the trustee was coded nowhere. Rule 1a applies to every row, and I report every result with and without it. Without it the count is six of seven, short of 0.9, so I say the interviews support the holder only under that rule.

EQ-app-L-eq2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-L-eq2.text: Several of your alphas are below Krippendorff's bar.

MA-app-L-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-L-eq2.text: Yes: penalty .54, stage .59, flows .55, what crosses .65. I report each pass separately rather than merging them, and the results I lean on use the firm codes: holder class .88, rivalry among co-users .85, neutral holder .84, market commonality .84. Every disagreement was listed and settled with its reason recorded (L.2, L.3).

EQ-app-L-eq3.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-L-eq3.text: How independent were the two coding passes?

MA-app-L-eq3.speaker: marigold
MA-app-L-eq3.text: Each version-3 pass was made from Appendix H and the transcripts, without sight of the earlier codes or of the other pass, to my written codebook, and every decision was logged and checked by me (3.2, 3.4, L.1). Version 2 was also coded twice, independently, over all 117 rows.

EQ-app-L-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-L-eq4.text: Why use QCA on so few cases?

MA-app-L-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-L-eq4.text: Because the question is which conditions are present wherever the outcome is, and crisp-set QCA asks exactly that. I use the conventional thresholds, 0.8 for sufficiency, re-run at 0.75 and 0.9, and 0.9 for necessity; I drop each case in turn and recode every helper and public body as never neutral. The two passes are run as replications, so a result has to hold in both (3.4).

EQ-app-L-eq5.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-L-eq5.text: Is there a case your condition can't explain?

MA-app-L-eq5.speaker: marigold
MA-app-L-eq5.text: Yes, H2-56: two bike couriers who, asked separately for quotes by the same city, came together and made a joint bid with no wall and no penalty. I report it as the exception rather than explain it away (L.4).

EQ-app-L-eq6.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-L-eq6.text: Why does L.6 count 36 neutral-third-party rows when Table H.3 says 35?

MA-app-L-eq6.speaker: marigold
MA-app-L-eq6.text: L.6 groups Appendix H's 'Bound by' column by keyword, while Table H.3 assigns one primary binder to each row by hand, so the counts differ by a row or two. I give both side by side (L.6; 4.4).

EL-council_office-WFB1.text: Overclaims. It is a worked example, not a forecast.

EL-council_office-WFB2.speaker: grill
EL-council_office-WFB2.text: Over-concedes. It shows the order of magnitude and which inputs drive it.

EL-CARD-app-N-what.speaker: marigold
EL-CARD-app-N-what.text: A worked example of what the proposed rule, checking that shared parcel points are neutral, might cost and save in one imaginary council area of 50,000 households, with every input and formula shown.

EL-CARD-app-N-why.speaker: marigold
EL-CARD-app-N-why.text: Backs 3.5 (the scenario method: low, central and high values, a worst case, only the increment counted, £7.08 an hour and 0.167 kg CO2e a kilometre) and 6.3 (the central net value of about £262,000; a check costing about £400 to £1,500 a point a year).

AF-N-f1.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f1.text: One notional council area of 50,000 households; a worked example, not a forecast.

AF-N-f2.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f2.text: Thirteen inputs, each with low, central and high values; eight are assumptions (P, d, r0, r, c, L, dt and N), and s and k are partly assumed.

AF-N-f3.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f3.text: Time is valued at the Department for Transport's non-work value and car emissions at the government's average-car factor.

AF-N-f4.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f4.text: Central case: 280,000 failed first attempts, 84,000 depot trips, 33,600 trips avoided, 28,000 hours saved.

AF-N-f5.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f5.text: Central case money: time worth £198,240, carrier saving £105,840, check cost £42,000 (60 points at £700), net £262,080 a year.

AF-N-f6.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f6.text: Low case net −£12,000; stress case (low benefits, high check cost) −£150,000 a year; high case net £1,719,000.

AF-N-f7.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f7.text: CO2 saved is 28.1 tonnes in the central case and 243.2 in the high; it is reported, not priced.

AF-N-f8.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f8.text: Only the increment over today's redirection is counted: trips avoided equal depot trips times (r minus r0).

AF-N-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f9.text: Households without a car (23.3%) account for about 7,829 of the central avoided trips and about 9,134 hours.

AF-N-f10.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f10.text: For a carrier, the expected cost per parcel is £1.82 at the door against £0.45 to £0.95 at a neutral point.

AF-N-f11.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f11.text: The check cost per point is built from Charnwood Borough Council's officer cost of £306.51 to £423.55 per licence plus about 24 test parcels at about £4.

AF-N-f12.speaker: marigold
AF-N-f12.text: The result turns on two inputs: the share of failures redirected (r) and the time saved per trip (dt).

EQ-app-N-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-N-eq1.text: Most of your inputs are assumptions. What is this scenario worth?

MA-app-N-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-N-eq1.text: It shows the order of magnitude and which inputs drive it, the share redirected and the time saved, and nothing more. Eight of the thirteen inputs are assumptions and I say so; the UK publishes no official first-attempt failure rate and I found no UK data on depot trips. The proper test is the matched-streets design I propose for further research (N.5).

MA-app-N-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-N-eq2.text: Yes. In the low case it adds nothing and the council is £12,000 down; in the stress case, low benefits with 100 points checked at £1,500 each, it's £150,000 down a year. The central case is about £262,000 net. I show all of them (N.3; 6.3).

EQ-app-N-eq3.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-N-eq3.text: Why don't you price the carbon?

MA-app-N-eq3.speaker: marigold
MA-app-N-eq3.text: I report it, 28.1 tonnes a year in the central case, but I don't price it, so the net figure is only residents' time and carriers' savings minus the cost of checking (N.2, N.3).

EQ-app-N-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-N-eq4.text: Aren't you counting redirection that already happens?

MA-app-N-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-N-eq4.text: No. Only the increment counts: trips avoided are depot trips times r minus r0, the share redirected under the rule minus the share already redirected today (N.2).

EQ-app-N-eq5.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-N-eq5.text: Lockers can be worse than the doorstep if people drive to them.

MA-app-N-eq5.speaker: marigold
MA-app-N-eq5.text: They can, as Niemeijer and Buijs found, which is why the rule is limited to shared points in towns within a five-minute walk (N.5).

QZ-app-N-q1.text: How many households does the notional council area have?

QZ-app-N-q7.text: What does the check cost per point a year, across the three cases?

EL-CARD-app-H-what.speaker: marigold
EL-CARD-app-H-what.text: A row-by-row ledger of every collaboration the interviewees described, 117 rows: who was involved, whether they competed, what they pooled and kept back, what held it together, who started it and what became of it.

EL-CARD-app-H-why.speaker: marigold
EL-CARD-app-H-why.text: The evidence base for Chapter 4: 3.1 and 3.4 (the arrangement as unit of analysis), 4.1 (117 rows), 4.3 (Table 4.5, what was pooled and withheld), 4.4 (95 of 117 bound from outside the parties; Table 4.6, the twenty-three failures), 4.5 (42 begun by a city or public body, 19 by a carrier), 4.7, 5.3, 6.1, 7.2 and 7.5; also 1.5 (the two peer-trust exceptions, rows 4 and 42 of H.1).

AF-H-f1.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f1.text: 117 rows: 56 from the A half (Table H.1) and 61 from the B half (Table H.2).

AF-H-f2.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f2.text: The unit is the description, not the scheme: a scheme described by two people is two rows, so the A half's 56 rows hold 51 to 52 unique schemes.

AF-H-f3.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f3.text: The A half's first listing held 39 accounts of 37 arrangements; H.1 adds 17 rows that listing left out, proposals and second descriptions among them.

AF-H-f4.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f4.text: Primary binder per row: neutral third party 35, grant 21, regulation or permit 17, contract 12, client mandate 5, prior vertical relationship 3, reciprocal trade 1, platform reputation 1: 95 bound from outside the parties.

AF-H-f5.speaker: marigold

AF-H-f6.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f6.text: Of the ten rows with no external binding agent, five failed outright.

AF-H-f7.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f7.text: Who began each row: city or public body 42, platform or broker 20, carrier 19, shipper or receiver 15, academic project 14, city with a project 1, could not be placed 6.

AF-H-f8.speaker: marigold

AF-H-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f9.text: Of the 35 rows bound by a neutral third party, 19 were operating, 10 were proposals, 2 pilots, 2 ended and 2 could not be placed.

AF-H-f10.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f10.text: Table H.4 gives 23 failed and unrealised arrangements in the participants' own words, with timestamps.

AF-H-f11.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f11.text: Coding B's first binder tally summed to 58 of 61 with double counting; it was rewritten on 16 September 2026 as a one-to-one assignment summing to 61.

AF-H-f12.speaker: marigold
AF-H-f12.text: A city's covenant of 40 companies promised data sharing; four years later the city officer still had no data.

EQ-app-H-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-H-eq1.text: You have 117 rows, but how many actual schemes?

MA-app-H-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-H-eq1.text: Fewer, and I say so. The unit is the description, so a scheme two people described is two rows, cross-referenced. The A half's 56 rows hold 51 to 52 unique schemes. A count of rows is a count of accounts of arrangements, and where the text needs the number of schemes it says so (3.1; note after Table H.2).

EQ-app-H-eq2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-H-eq2.text: Your 95 of 117 rests on a binder you assigned once. Where's the reliability figure?

MA-app-H-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-H-eq2.text: That's a real limit and I state it in 3.4 and 3.7. The binder and the initiator were assigned once, by hand, when I built the appendix, so the binder carries no agreement figure. The initiator was re-checked in both coding passes of October 2026 and read the same way in 98 of 117 rows, alpha .80. And the rule for what counts as a binder is written down and applied to both halves (note on 'peer trust alone').

EQ-app-H-eq3.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-H-eq3.text: Four rows run on peer trust alone. Don't they contradict you?

MA-app-H-eq3.speaker: marigold
MA-app-H-eq3.text: They're the cases the claim has to answer, and I list each with what became of it: a rural case that's only the participant's inference (H.1, 42); a dairy and a vegetable supplier who don't compete (H.1, 52); four friends' cargo-bike cooperative that dissolved (H.2, 33); and two bike couriers' joint bid, which is the one case that worked between rivals at the door (H.2, 56).

EQ-app-H-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-H-eq4.text: Why should we believe failures that are only reported in interviews?

MA-app-H-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-H-eq4.text: They're accounts, not measured deliveries, and I treat them as that. But every failure in Table H.4 is in the participant's own words with its timestamp, so it can be checked against the transcript. And the pattern is stark: five of the ten rows with no outside binder failed outright.

EQ-app-H-eq5.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-H-eq5.text: What exactly do you mean by 'bound by'?

MA-app-H-eq5.speaker: marigold
MA-app-H-eq5.text: Whatever holds an arrangement together once it's formed and doesn't depend on the parties' goodwill. A platform that only made the introduction, or a procurement rule that only triggered it, isn't counted as a binder. That's why H.1 row 52 and H.2 row 56 stand as peer trust alone (note under Table H.3).

EL-CARD-app-B-why.speaker: marigold
EL-CARD-app-B-why.text: Backs 3.3, which says every participant received the sheet and the form approved with the guide, that twenty-seven of the thirty signed and three consented verbally on the recording; and 3.6, whose survey consent item asked respondents to confirm they had read this sheet.

EL-CARD-app-C-what.speaker: marigold
EL-CARD-app-C-what.text: The ethics application Khaled sent to the University, the record of its approval on 22 February 2024, and the draft survey he sent with it.

EL-CARD-app-C-why.speaker: marigold
EL-CARD-app-C-why.text: Backs 3.3 (approval as Category A on 22 February 2024, on condition that the supervisors approved the final questions), 3.6 (the survey ran under that approval; the application planned correlation and regression; the draft of 19 February 2024 is C.4) and 3.8, change 2 (the survey ran beside the interviews, not after them as the application planned).

AF-B-f1.speaker: marigold
AF-B-f1.text: Twenty-seven of the thirty participants returned the consent form signed.

AF-B-f2.speaker: marigold

AF-B-f6.text: The legal basis given for collecting the data.

AF-B-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-B-f9.text: The signed forms and the recordings are held by the author and not reproduced, because they carry names.

EQ-app-B-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-B-eq1.text: Three of your participants didn't sign the form. Is their consent valid?

MA-app-B-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-B-eq1.text: Yes. Every participant was sent the sheet and the form. Twenty-seven of the thirty signed. Three, A5, the second person in A9 and B8, gave consent verbally and it's on the recording; B8's came at the end of the call, and B8 had been sent the sheet, which says the interview would be recorded and that recording could be declined. EQ-app-B-eq2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-B-eq2.text: Your information sheet mentions the construction industry and calls you 'herself'. Was this really the sheet you used?

MA-app-B-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-B-eq2.text: Yes. It's reproduced exactly as approved and as participants received it, slips included. The construction sentence is left over from the University template and describes neither this research nor any use of its data. I point out every one of those slips myself in B.3 rather than tidy them away.

EQ-app-B-eq3.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-B-eq3.text: Item 6 of the consent form says the circumstances for breaking confidentiality are explained in the sheet. Where?

MA-app-B-eq3.speaker: marigold
MA-app-B-eq3.text: They aren't, and I say so in B.3. The form is reproduced as it was approved. In the thesis no participant and no employer is named, organisations are described by type, and participants appear only as codes (3.3).

EQ-app-B-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-B-eq4.text: How did you protect your participants' identities?

MA-app-B-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-B-eq4.text: Everyone is a code, A1 to A13 and B1 to B13. Organisations are described by type, roles that would narrow to one person are widened, and the eleven countries are given as a set, never against a code. A city or scheme is named only where it's public record and more than one person could have described it (3.3; G.1).

AF-C-f1.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f1.text: The application was submitted and approved on the same day, as Category A.

AF-C-f2.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f2.text: It was approved by the Chair of the School of Architecture and the Built Environment's ethics committee; the record is the Chair's comment in the University's virtual learning environment, with the name redacted.

AF-C-f3.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f3.text: Approval carried one condition, which was met: the final questions had to be approved by the supervisory team before primary data collection.

AF-C-f4.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f4.text: The project title on the application differs from the thesis title.

AF-C-f5.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f5.text: The application planned a mixed-methods design: a systematic review, interviews, case studies and surveys.

AF-C-f6.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f6.text: The application planned to build the survey on the findings of the qualitative phase and to analyse it by correlation and regression.

AF-C-f7.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f7.text: The application planned to validate the framework through expert panels drawn from earlier participants.

AF-C-f8.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f8.text: The draft survey is dated 19 February 2024, has thirteen questions in five sections and says it takes 10 to 15 minutes.

AF-C-f9.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f9.text: The draft told companies that do not collaborate to skip past the questions for collaborators.

AF-C-f10.speaker: marigold
AF-C-f10.text: The draft's longest duration was 'More than 3 years'; the final form recorded 'More than 5 years'.

EQ-app-C-eq1.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-C-eq1.text: Your application promised correlation and regression on the survey. Why didn't you run them?

MA-app-C-eq1.speaker: marigold
MA-app-C-eq1.text: Because the sample selected itself through my networks, and a self-selected sample supports no estimate beyond itself, as Fowler says. So I read the survey descriptively, for scale, in counts and cross-tabulations, and run no test of significance. The plan is reproduced in C.1 so anyone can see what was promised, and the change is recorded in 3.6 and in Table 3.8 as change 2.

EQ-app-C-eq2.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-C-eq2.text: The application said the survey would follow the interviews, but it opened the day you were approved. Why?

MA-app-C-eq2.speaker: marigold
MA-app-C-eq2.text: That's right, and it's the second change in Table 3.8. The form opened on 22 February 2024 on the draft's questions as my supervisors approved them, and it ran until 30 April 2025, beside the interviews. So it asks about the four pillars, not the five links, and no link of the chain rests on it.

EQ-app-C-eq3.speaker: dr_tally
EQ-app-C-eq3.text: Approval came the same day you submitted. Was the review adequate?

MA-app-C-eq3.speaker: marigold
MA-app-C-eq3.text: It went through the Faculty's postgraduate research ethics process and was approved as Category A by the Chair of the School's ethics committee, with a condition that my supervisors approve the final questions before data collection, which was done. The record is the Chair's comment in the University's virtual learning environment, reproduced in C.2 with the Chair's name redacted (C.3).

EQ-app-C-eq4.speaker: prof_kerbstone
EQ-app-C-eq4.text: Your application mentioned case studies and validation by expert panels. Where are they?

MA-app-C-eq4.speaker: marigold
MA-app-C-eq4.text: The thesis reports neither. Ghent is read as a document analysis, not a case study in Yin's sense, which would have needed the operators and the permit register as well as the plans (3.5). And the framework is offered as propositions, each of two variables, for others to test, rather than validated by a panel (3.1). Table 3.8 records five changes of instrument and answer; these two planned elements weren't carried through, and I'd say so plainly.

QZ-app-C-q1.speaker: marigold
QZ-app-C-q1.text: On what date was the ethics application approved?
